#5858. The next wave of energy storage capacity is already on the grid

Next week, much of the industry will gather in Las Vegas for RE+ to talk about what gets built next. It’s an important conversation, but I’d encourage asset owners to bring a second question with them: what more can we get from what’s already been built?

This question matters more than ever as electricity demand climbs and customers feel it on their monthly bill. EIA expects consumption to grow another 3.1% in 2027, driven largely by data centers and other commercial loads, while residential customers will pay nearly 5% more for power this year.

The industry is working hard to add capacity, but getting it built takes time. According to Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory and GridTracker, the median project built in 2025 spent more than five years moving from interconnection request to commercial operation and only 13% of the capacity that requested interconnection between 2000 and 2020 had come online by the end of 2025. New generation is essential, but the fleet already operating is an opportunity we can’t afford to pass up.

With nearly 52 gigawatts (GW) of utility-scale battery storage operating in the U.S. as of mid-2026, the installed base is too large to overlook and performance across it varies widely. When a battery energy storage system (BESS) falls short, the instinct is often to blame the battery and reach for augmentation or replacement, but in many cases the bottleneck is the controls, software and integration around it.

Higher prices should raise the value of delivering power when and where the grid needs it, yet revenues for many operating assets are moving in the other direction. In ERCOT, the average battery earned 84% less in 2025 than at its 2023 peak, as more storage competed for the same services. With incentive economics shifting too, asset managers face real pressure to get more from existing assets.

At the same time, utilities are leaning on storage for grid stability. As more gas units face revenue pressure and retirement, the grid loses the spinning mass that provides inertia in the first moments of a disturbance. Grid-forming inverters can replace that inertia, often by upgrading existing storage rather than building new. Providing that support, alongside peak shaving, load shifting and voltage and frequency regulation, takes controls that respond faster than many legacy SCADA and EMS platforms were built to handle.

Compliance requirements are moving just as quickly, with FERC Order No. 901 directing NERC to develop new reliability standards for inverter-based resources, including batteries, through 2030. Many plants operating today were designed before those requirements existed, increasing the importance of controls that can evolve as grid codes change. The same logic also applies to solar and wind plants. Once control functions are proven in the field they can easily be applied to other assets across the whole market.

A recent Gridmatic study of 30 California batteries shows what’s at stake, with fleetwide availability averaging just under 80% and execution and bidding strategy driving a wide gap between top and bottom performers. Had every asset matched the leader, the group would have earned an estimated $98 million more over two years. The lesson isn't that every performance gap can be solved with software. It's that owners shouldn't assume the battery itself is the limiting factor.

Before committing additional capital, owners should examine the full system: controls, software, market strategy, integration and plant-level coordination alongside battery health and hardware performance.

Think about the smartphone in your pocket. Its hardware may be several years old, but software updates can improve how it performs and add capabilities that weren’t available when you bought it. Storage assets aren't so different: the physical equipment may still have years of useful life, while the controls and software around it can evolve to meet new market and grid requirements.

A modern energy management and plant control platform layered onto existing assets can help owners:

We saw this firsthand in the U.K., where our team, then part of Wärtsilä, worked with Zenobē to retrofit an existing 100 MW/100 MWh battery site with a new GEMS power plant controller. The upgrade took over energy management, secured grid compliance and added stateful grid-code functions such as de-load, along with control for multiple tenants sharing one point of interconnection.

The batteries stayed in place, but the site gained new capabilities and is better prepared for future requirements. That same approach translates to U.S. markets, where interconnection rules and local regulations are evolving quickly.

New deployments will remain critical, but the next wave of value may come from making today’s fleet work harder. As the industry gathers at RE+, owners should ask not just what they need to build next, but what more the assets already on the grid could deliver. Before replacing hardware or adding capacity, diagnose the whole plant. The constraint may not be the battery cells.

#5856. XPENG Researchers and Academic Partners Introduce GroundingPI, An Open-Source Visual Perception Model For Physical AI

Guangzhou, China — XPENG (NYSE: XPEV, HKEX: 9868), a leading Physical AI company, has supported the development of GroundingPI, an open-source visual perception foundation model created by researchers affiliated with XPENG, Peking University, The University of Hong Kong and other academic institutions.

The research explores a new approach to embodied intelligence by focusing on a fundamental capability: enabling AI systems to accurately identify objects and understand their spatial positions in the physical world. With approximately 4 billion parameters, GroundingPI achieved the highest aggregate score among 44 baseline models evaluated across 34 perception benchmarks covering 11 capability categories.

The research paper, model weights and supporting code have been made publicly available, enabling researchers and developers to further explore perception-focused approaches to Physical AI.

As AI increasingly moves beyond digital environments into physical applications such as robotics and autonomous driving, accurately understanding the surrounding environment becomes essential.

While general-purpose foundation models have demonstrated strong capabilities in language understanding, reasoning and planning, physical intelligence requires more precise visual perception. AI systems must not only recognize objects but also identify their exact locations and spatial relationships to support real-world interaction.

GroundingPI takes a perception-focused approach to this challenge. Rather than relying on robot action labels during the perceptual model’s training, the research focuses on developing foundational visual understanding capabilities that can support downstream action-learning systems.

For example, when instructed to identify “the handle of the cup on the right”, an AI system needs to locate not only the correct cup but also the precise position of its handle. GroundingPI is designed to represent such information using spatial coordinates, including points and bounding boxes.

The model is trained across 11 categories of perceptual capabilities, including object detection, dense object localization, referring expression grounding, optical character recognition (OCR), document layout understanding, user interface element recognition and robotic spatial localization.

By strengthening these fundamental capabilities, the research explores how specialized perception models could provide a more effective visual foundation for embodied AI systems.

In evaluations conducted by the research team, GroundingPI was compared with 44 baseline models across 34 public perception benchmarks spanning 11 capability categories.

Using an aggregate evaluation score with equal weighting across the capability categories, GroundingPI achieved 73.68, compared with 71.54 for GPT-6 Astra.

The results demonstrate the potential of specialized perception-focused models to outperform larger general-purpose models on specific visual grounding tasks. The comparison relates to the evaluated perception benchmarks and does not represent a broader assessment of general AI intelligence or reasoning capabilities.

GroundingPI’s performance was particularly relevant to tasks requiring precise object localization, including complex visual scenes containing numerous objects or small targets.

These findings suggest that targeted perceptual pretraining can provide a valuable foundation for future Physical AI research, complementing the broader reasoning and planning capabilities of general-purpose foundation models.

Beyond perception benchmarks, the research team evaluated GroundingPI as a visual foundation for downstream robotic manipulation and autonomous driving tasks.

The results highlight two potential advantages for embodied intelligence.

Robotic systems often require extensive human demonstrations to learn new manipulation tasks, creating significant challenges in data collection and training.

In RoboCasa-GR1 simulation experiments, robotic learning systems using GroundingPI as their visual backbone achieved higher task success rates with 50% of the available demonstration data than the evaluated comparison models trained with 75%.

This finding suggests that stronger foundational perception capabilities may reduce the amount of action-training data required for certain robotic tasks, potentially improving the efficiency of future embodied AI development.

Another major challenge in robotics is generalization: the ability to perform a learned task when objects, backgrounds or environmental conditions change.

In RoboTwin 2.0 simulation evaluations, GroundingPI demonstrated stronger performance than the evaluated mainstream visual backbones across four out-of-distribution settings, indicating improved adaptability to unfamiliar environments.

The research team also evaluated its potential for autonomous driving perception using the nuScenes dataset. When integrated as a visual backbone, GroundingPI achieved an average open-loop trajectory prediction error of 0.296 metres in the reported evaluation.

Together, these experimental findings highlight the potential of perception-focused foundation models to support more adaptable and data-efficient embodied intelligence systems.

The research remains exploratory. Its downstream results are based on simulation and offline evaluations and do not establish readiness for real-world commercial deployment.

GroundingPI explores a research direction in which specialized visual perception capabilities complement higher-level reasoning and planning, rather than relying exclusively on general-purpose models for every component of an embodied intelligence system.

The findings provide insights into how perception-focused pretraining could contribute to future research on robotic manipulation, autonomous driving and other applications requiring precise interaction with the physical world.

To encourage further exploration and collaboration, the research team has made GroundingPI’s paper, model weights and supporting code publicly accessible, subject to the applicable open-source and third-party licensing terms.

The project represents an academic research contribution supported by XPENG and its research collaborators. The results do not constitute an announcement of integration into XPENG’s commercial products or a commitment to future deployment.

Project Website: https://groundingpi.github.io/ Research Paper: https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.39601 Source Code: https://github.com/groundingpi/GroundingPI Model Weights: https://huggingface.co/GroundingPI/GroundingPI

XPENG is a leading global Physical AI company, dedicated to bringing artificial intelligence into the physical world to reshape future mobility and smart living. Through in-house R&D, XPENG has developed a full-stack Physical AI architecture spanning Turing AI chips, world foundation models, and highly integrated software and hardware applications. This unified technology foundation of XPENG powers an expansive product portfolio of smart EVs, robotaxis, and humanoid robots, advancing the deployment of Physical AI at scale.

Headquartered in Guangzhou, China, XPENG is dual-primary listed on the New York Stock Exchange and the Hong Kong Stock Exchange. With global capabilities across R&D, manufacturing, sales, and services, XPENG drives continuous technological innovation and fosters an open Physical AI ecosystem, making life smarter, safer, and better for users worldwide. For more information, please visit https://www.xpeng.com/.

#5854. New York program funds $13 million in energy storage advancement projects

New York State’s Power Generation and Storage Innovation program has awarded nearly $13 million to 15 projects to support product development and demonstration of scalable long duration and other advanced battery energy storage solutions.

“Investing in next-generation energy storage technologies is critical to building a flexible and resilient grid that can make the most of our diverse energy resources,” said Doreen M. Harris, NYSERDA president and CEO. “These projects will advance promising solutions that can deliver power when it is needed most, strengthen grid performance and help drive down costs as we build a more affordable and reliable energy system for New York consumers.”

NYSERDA’s Power Generation and Storage Innovation program awards projects that develop and demonstrate innovative long duration energy storage (LDES) and other under-utilized, alternatives to traditional lithium-ion technologies. The awarded technologies include new designs for scalable LDES solutions that are over 10 hours in duration at rated power and will address cost, performance, and integration challenges such as grid congestion, hosting capacity constraints and lithium-ion siting limitations.

Public Service Commission Chair Rory Christian said, “Storage is poised to play an increasingly critical role in supporting a reliable, cost-effective, flexible, and lower emissions system as more clean energy resources are integrated into the grid, as well as enhance the efficiency of the state’s existing resources. NYSERDA’s dedication of these funds originating from innovation and research funding overseen by the Commission positions New York’s consumers to yield the promising long-term benefits expected by more complex and scalable applications of these technologies.”

All contracts are awarded to companies located in New York, partnered with New York companies or for development and demonstrations in the state. Today’s announcement supports NYSERDA’s Innovation and Research (I&R) program, which invests over $96 million per year to attract world-class energy innovators, reduce risk for private investors and remove barriers to clean energy adoption in New York State, leveraging $15 in additional investment for every $1 spent. NYSERDA has partnered with over 900 companies that have helped make more than 300 products commercially available for consumers, businesses and utilities.

Power Generation and Storage Innovation funding for comes from the state’s Clean Energy Fund.

#5853. Every virtual megawatt needs a meter

Last month, Google announced a deal with Voltus for a virtual power plant (VPP) of up to 1,070 MW in PJM, roughly the output of a large nuclear reactor. Rather than build a plant, Voltus will offer homes and businesses financial incentives to trim usage when the grid is strained, through smart thermostats, batteries and flexible equipment.

The deal represents an inflection point for the power and utilities sector, where “speed to power” innovations are defining the moment. It also underscores the importance of the equipment that will decide how far such programs go: the electric meter.

NEMA's 2026 Grid Reliability Study projects U.S. economy-wide electricity demand as much as 55% by 2050, with data center consumption alone growing 300% over the next decade. New generation and transmission can't keep pace, as permitting, capital needs and equipment and skilled labor backlogs protracting project delivery timelines.

As a result, operators are looking for capacity in the system they already have. On the transmission side, grid-enhancing technologies show what's possible: PJM modeling finds they could unlock between six and seven GW of usable capacity.

At the grid edge, the opportunity may be larger. Demand response contributed 33.3 GW of enrolled wholesale capacity in 2024, about 6.5% of peak demand in organized markets and could reach 20% of U.S. peak by 2030. Behind-the-meter resources, which include microgrids and aggregations of customer-sited resources (i.e., VPPs), are scaling too.

What these grid-edge resources share is a need for measurement. A demand response event or VPP dispatch only has value if someone can prove the load dropped and pay the customer who dropped it. That job falls to the electric meter.

Despite the momentum, only 6.5% of U.S. electricity customers are enrolled in retail demand response programs. NEMA's research points to several reasons: metering and communication rules written for large power plants that burden small participants, too little public data on how flexible resources perform during grid emergencies and market rules that vary by region.

Underneath them is a question of trust. Some grid operators and utilities still doubt that distributed resources will deliver when called. But confidence at scale requires consistent, verifiable measurement across millions of devices and many vendors.

That is the role of ANSI NEMA C12.1-2026. C12.1 sets performance criteria for new types of watthour and demand meters, defines accuracy classes and test methods and establishes acceptable in-service performance for revenue meters. When a meter reading decides whether a customer is paid for curtailment, or whether an operator can count an aggregation as capacity, those criteria make the number credible.

Timing makes this pressing. Millions of first-generation smart meters, many installed between 2010 and 2015 with American Recovery and Reinvestment Act funding, are reaching end of life. Utilities in every region are planning or executing large-scale replacements through the late 2020s, driven by aging hardware, obsolete communications and the need to support distributed energy resources, EVs and resilience. Indeed, as NEMA member company Honeywell has noted, first-wave meters lack the speed and accuracy of newer models and networks and security practices evolve faster than meters can be replaced. This is a replacement market, not a first deployment and the meters chosen now will likely stay in service for 15 to 20 years or more.

The 2026 edition of C12.1 arrives at the right moment. It folds the former C12.20 accuracy-class standard into a single document covering the entire metering code and adds guidance on non-Blondel metering. Referencing C12.1-2026 in procurement specifications gives utilities, regulators and vendors a common baseline for safety, accuracy and interoperability across vendors and networks and protects ratepayers' two-decade investment.

The same long-term lens applies to where grid equipment comes from. NEMA's Make It American® program is an industry-led, third party-certification program. Accredited auditors evaluate manufacturers against the NEMA 70901-2026 process standard and certified facilities and products are listed in a public Build America, Buy America registry. The Federal Highway Administration and the Texas, Arkansas and Montana transportation departments recognize it and a pending bill in the U.S. Senate features language treating Make It American documentation as sufficient evidence of domestic-content compliance.

NEMA has prioritized product-level specifications for the equipment utilities buy most, including high- and medium-voltage distribution equipment, grid management and automation equipment and wire and cable. That lets procurement teams verify domestic content product-by-product, with certification that reflects actual production practices.

Virtual power plants may be the fastest new capacity on the market. But a virtual megawatt is only as real as the meter that proves it was delivered.

#5852. Thermal Dawn — Thermal Storage Is Cheap Storage

Another great idea from Down Under: Thermal Dawn promises cost effective heating and cooling, mainly by replacing gas boilers in cold climates. CleanTechnica had a chance to interview Nick Zeniou, Founder of Thermal Dawn, recently by phone, fresh after his presentation at Everything Electric. You can hear him explain his revolutionary system here, or here with a little less drama.

Everything Electric was a good opportunity to measure public reaction to the new product. Nick tells me that hundreds of people checked out their stall. “People care about carbon cost and comfort. People don’t compromise on comfort.” Sounds like comfort trumps carbon cost. Homeowners who visited the stand and filled out the survey were focused on sustainability and cost. Nick cautions: “it was an electrification expo crowd, and 50 of the 62 already had solar, so it’s not the whole market.” See the chart below.

Although I live in the warmer part of Australia (Brisbane), many Aussies have to endure cold winters. Nick tells me he is looking at installs in Sydney, Canberra, and Melbourne in the deep south. Thermal Dawn can store heat up to 70 degrees Celsius, or down to 5 degrees. Thermal Dawns’ equipment can run cold or hot water through pipes and radiators that are already installed, depending on the need — without having to run an expensive gas boiler. He describes it as a thermal battery. Just to be clear, it does not generate electricity.

Check out this graph below, which shows the Thermal Dawn system in action at a house in Melbourne during a day in August 2026. It shows room temperature and when the heat pump was running, in 15-minute samples, unedited. The heat pump ran until about 1:45pm, then not again, heated by stored energy through the evening peak.

“What about return on investment,” I asked. He described two systems they have had running over the southern Australian winter which have saved the homeowners approximately AU$1,500 each. “The first was a house in Melbourne, our first install, live since May 2026. The owners charge the system in their retailer’s free three-hour midday window, so the heat for the evening costs them close to nothing. The second was a Warragul (slab-heated home, Victoria): installed in two days in July 2026. Our controls turn the home’s concrete slab into part of the battery, managing when it charges and when it releases heat. On 95% of winter evenings, the heat pumps did not run at all between 5 pm and 9pm. Since commissioning, 70,521 MJ of gas has been avoided by just these two installations.”

Nick further explains: “A standard heat pump draws from the grid during those expensive morning and evening hours. You’ve escaped gas, but you’re still paying premium rates every time the temperature drops at night. Thermal Dawn is different. Our system charges when power is cheapest, a free midday window, your own solar, or late-night off-peak, then delivers that stored warmth through your radiators and underfloor heating all evening, with the compressor off through the expensive hours.

It appears that Thermal Dawn’s secret sauce is “Phase Change Materials.” Naturally, Nick declined to share exactly what Thermal Dawn is using. The system replaces a gas boiler with a combination of reverse cycle heat pump, well insulated water tank, and phase change materials. PCMs are designed to freeze or melt at a specific temperature, storing and releasing heat when they change physical state, usually from solid to liquid. “PCM doubles our heat capacity.” The heating applications I could understand, what about the cooling? “Cool water from the tank runs through a fan coil unit, and the fan blows cool air into the room. Cooling is an optional add-on.” That’s the answer.

How do thermal storage and a home battery/solar system work together? “Thermal storage is cheap storage doing one job very well. Heating, cooling, and hot water are the largest, most predictable loads in the house, and covering them thermally is far cheaper per kWh than covering them from lithium. A battery is expensive storage doing a general-purpose job.

“The practical effect is that your battery stops being the thing that carries your heating. It’s freed up for lights, appliances, the EV, and overnight backup, and it lasts longer for not being cycled hard every winter evening. Homes with a battery already are often the clearest case, because the expensive storage stops being spent on the cheapest possible job.”

Thermal dawn connects to existing hydronic pipework. The gas boiler with its high gas bills is gone. Check out the animation of heat discharge overnight. “The thermal battery charged on solar during the day and now heats the house while the heat pump stays off. It’s an illustration of what the app shows, not a recording of a live home.” For those rooms that don’t have hydronic radiators or underfloor slab heating, Thermal Dawn installs fan coil units. Nick tells me via a followup email that: “It’s a small indoor unit with a water coil and a fan: warm water from the thermal battery runs through the coil, and the fan blows the heating or cooling into the room.”

The heavy technical discussion out of the way, I asked Nick about his background. He grew up in an isolated part of New Zealand. His job was to collect the firewood for the family’s heat source — a fireplace. He had to get the fire going by 4:00 pm or the house would not warm up for the cold evening. Timing was very important, as it is for electricity use.

Nick is a mechanical engineer who has worked across tech companies and startups. While working on installing commercial air conditioning, he came across the idea that became Thermal Dawn. Nick joined the dots between the huge variations in electricity supply cost throughout each 24-hour period, with an average home’s thermal energy needs (up to two-thirds of consumption) and the fact that homes are becoming power stations. Thence to thermal batteries powered by Thermal Dawn technology.

He reminisces about the start of the business: “When our first unit was finished, we loaded it into a ute at 5pm and I drove it down the Hume overnight, Sydney to Melbourne (1000 km), to install it the next morning. We had a four-month-old at home at the time. My wife Linda is my co-founder and leads mechanical design and manufacturing, so while I was on the road, she was looking after a newborn.”

For those who would like to get involved, Nick invites Australian homeowners to sign up here and they’ll be in touch. “Readers overseas: send us a message or request a quote at the same link to register interest. If we hear from enough people in one area, we can bring forward our plans to come there.”

Having proven their point, Thermal Dawn is cleared to sell and installing its first batch now, with a larger product for ducted air conditioning in development. I asked about apartment block heating and Nick confirmed that they are looking at it but want to get the domestic home sorted first.

I asked a couple of followup questions “What about the Victorian government’s position?” Nick’s answer:  “Victoria is set to bring in support for systems like ours from the middle of next year. With the state election in November, there’s talk of a change in direction and of belt-tightening, so we’ve built Thermal Dawn to stand on its own. It saves households money without a subsidy, and any support is a bonus.”

Any plans for installs in Canberra? “Yes. Canberra is one of the best places in Australia for this: cold winters, plenty of hydronic homes, and a territory already moving off gas. We’re talking with installers there now.”

I really appreciate these technological experts when they take the time to explain things to me. Sometimes I feel like Winnie the Pooh — a bear of very little brain. Looks like Thermal Dawn has solved another part of the energy puzzle — good news for homeowners and also for the planet.

#5850. How Can Europe Accelerate Electric Trucking?

Europe is having a hard time lately, with skyrocketing oil prices dampening economies. Fuel costs, particularly diesel, are prompting surging interest in truck electrification. Europe has been urging truck makers to move toward electric trucking, and they have responded with a variety of electric semi trucks from many manufacturers. Europe is a group of sovereign countries with many standards. The European Union is a political and economic union of 27 states in that area. It issued directives urging action and imposing penalties. In response to European Union directives, companies have formed EV100, a coalition of corporations responding to the need. In a recent story, Steve Hanley wrote about European electric truck makers’ difficulties expanding truck electrification. Here’s a quotation from the story: “In a letter to EU Commission president Ursula von der Leyen, of primary concern, in their estimation, is expanding the charging infrastructure for heavy-duty trucks in Europe.” There is no shortage of electric trucks in Europe. Expansion could go faster were it not for charging infrastructure. Manufacturers complain about “an alarming delay” in conditions needed to drive market uptake. For Europe, truck electrification is not working as well as in China, where over 90% of the world’s electric trucks reside. The differences between China and the EU show some reasons why truck electrification is slower in Europe. How did China succeed where the EU failed? China made electric trucks a freight system, not a vehicle category.

Power is a major factor in electric grid infrastructure. Charging electric trucks places demands on power. Peak power determines how much infrastructure is necessary. In grid planning, peak annual power determines how much capital equipment is necessary. Reducing peak power demand is a critical factor for electric truck infrastructure. Figure 1 shows one method of reducing power called route stuffing. It schedules departures on heavy traffic corridors at regularly spaced intervals. Corridors like ones between ports and warehouses are a target for those practices. These corridors often route trucks in a round trip chain. Filling routes with scheduled trips can reduce power demand compared to random trip scheduling. The article Battery Swap Uses Fewer Batteries Than You Think is devoted to methods of analysis and planning that can lead to lower peak power demand. There are other benefits to planning, such as greater truck load capacity from the same amount of batteries. Part of the solution to slow electric truck infrastructure development is to plan infrastructure and truck use practices to reduce the charging power burden. Given the pressing and enduring need due to the diesel fuel cost crisis, it is necessary to reprioritize grid power upgrade demands. Demands for data center power upgrades like transformers for substations should be re shuffled and prioritized toward the diesel crisis.

In two articles, Michael Barnard outlined the issues. Vehicles are not a transportation system. What does Europe have now? It has an EU Commission interacting with a coalition, EV100. The problem is, there are plenty of trucks available, but who is in charge of infrastructure? You can’t have electric trucks without means of charging, but as the coalition complains, “Significant improvements to charging infrastructure, a reduction in carbon dioxide based tolls, and a coherent policy framework are urgently needed.” There are so many stakeholders — including the commission, vehicles makers, and charging companies across multiple countries — that no one is in charge of infrastructure, and without it, nothing moves. It needs a unity of purpose and action.

If China is succeeding, why not adopt its strategy? Perhaps the answer is right in front of everyone’s nose. As Michael puts it, “the policy connects vehicles to corridors, depots, service areas, grids and freight use cases instead of treating sales targets as sufficient.” CATL offered Europe a system, not a vehicle. This is a “turn key” solution. It’s a well thought out system, including use of methods and practices, not an anything goes free-for-all. That kind of stability and predictability is what EV100 leaders are looking for. This is not a swap-or-nothing scenario. Different techniques apply to various use cases. Swap must be planned for high-use freight corridors and other proper applications. Swap trucks can also fast charge or slow charge, providing flexibility and a system of trucks that includes smaller trucks, not just semis.

What does all this have to do with Europe’s slowly advancing infrastructure? Simply put, electric trucks put heavy charging demands on the grid. Trucks can have megawatt-hour batteries that require megawatt power charging to charge in an hour. Reducing grid power demands can reduce grid infrastructure upgrade costs, and leverage capital investment toward faster implementation.

“The process of getting megawatt charging equipment connected to the grid can take several years, delaying deployment even where operators and infrastructure providers are ready to invest.” The need for megawatt charging equipment is reduced by accelerating swap network development instead of fixed battery trucks that must be charged by fast chargers. “Swaptopus is easy to misread as a quirky name for another electric-truck infrastructure project. It is a newly formed joint venture between Octopus Energy and CATL, created to develop automated battery-swapping hubs for heavy trucks across Europe.” Unlike the government of China that played a role in encouraging standards and cooperation in infrastructure, Europe has a looser arrangement between many countries with various standards. Europe is learning the slow, hard way where battery swapping is most needed.

Every truck application has different optimization. It means that there must be different approaches to fit freight operations in heavy traffic corridors. Quoting Michael Barnard, “Freight operators often run repeated routes between ports, factories, distribution centres and logistics hubs. Those patterns provide known traffic, known stopping points and relatively predictable electricity demand. A swap hub can be placed around an existing freight flow instead of hoping that enough unrelated trucks eventually pass through.”

Freight corridors are a scenario made to order for battery swap. Real trucking solutions include a mix of vehicle and infrastructure types — from small, local delivery, to large, long-haul freight; and from slow, overnight charging, to medium power charging and battery swap — all used in concert to accelerate heavy truck electrification. With a wide variety of charging options, and vehicles and charging use cases targeted in coordination to avoid peak power demands, the path forward is eased. School buses don’t need expensive high-power fast charging. Lower-power chargers can do the trick. Local delivery can use a mix of overnight and medium power charging. Heavy truck dispatch must be more carefully coordinated to avoid peak demand and grid upgrade costs. A mix of medium-power charging and swap stations along with planned use cases can successfully lower electric freight power needs and transport system capital expenses to speed transport electrification.

Transformation and conversion of diesel freight systems to electric requires coordination and planning between government agencies and coalitions of corporations, cities, government agencies, and planners. Transportation is a system basic to societies and economics. Coordination between groups at all levels results in practices, use cases, and infrastructure that produce benefits for all. Grid expansion and construction can take years. In order for Europe to implement truck freight electrification, more structure and planning is needed to minimize grid power requirements, speed implementation, and maximize capital investment results. Transportation system, practices, and infrastructure must be planned for optimum results.

#5849. Oral Food Challenge Clears Many Infants Thought to Have Peanut Allergy

— Researchers say biomarkers and clinical history of reaction alone aren't enough for diagnosis

More than a third of infants thought to be allergic to peanuts were not actually allergic, an oral food challenge study showed.

With the aim of treating peanut allergy among babies who reacted to peanut before 1 year of age and had a positive skin prick or blood test, 34.8% who were subject to an oral food challenge (OFC) to set the dose for oral immunotherapy came up negative and could be considered non-allergic by this gold-standard test.

That rate was "far higher than expected," noted Kirsten Perrett, MBBS, PhD, of Murdoch Children's Research Institute at the Royal Children's Hospital in Melbourne, Australia, and colleagues in the Journal of Allergy and Clinical Immunology: In Practice.

Typically, a history of reaction plus sensitization is considered enough for diagnosis of peanut allergy, and children are sent home with instructions to avoid peanut products. While a majority of children outgrow milk or egg allergies, only about a quarter to a third of children outgrow peanut allergies without treatment by age 6 years.

The current results potentially indicate that some infants have a transient immune response to the allergen that resolves quickly (an average of 6 months between initial reaction and OFC in this study) or doesn't result in ongoing reactions upon further exposure, Perrett and team said.

Determining that early allows reintroduction of peanut in infancy, which may change the trajectory of peanut allergy and reduce the burden of food allergy, independent of an oral immunotherapy program, they added.

OFC "should be routinely considered in infant peanut allergy evaluation regardless of the proposed management strategy (immunotherapy or allergen avoidance)," Perrett and colleagues argued. "Biomarkers and clinical history alone are insufficient to diagnose peanut allergy in this age group."

That hasn't been the case "for a variety of reasons including carer or clinician concerns regarding safety, time, and/or resource constraints, or the belief that an OFC is unnecessary when there is a clear clinical history of reaction and a positive test of sensitization," they wrote.

With regard to safety, their study showed 61 cases of anaphylaxis during the 778 threshold OFCs (7.8%), which is a higher rate than in the conventional use of OFCs for cases in which diagnosis is unclear from clinical history or the allergy is suspected to be outgrown. While that means these OFCs should be performed in centers with appropriate medical support, the trade-off is worthwhile, Perrett and colleagues suggested.

"Accurately confirming allergy via OFC in infants can reduce the burden of allergy for patients, families, and society through misdiagnosis, and before the commencement of OIT [oral immunotherapy], it can help avoid unnecessary treatment," they pointed out.

The Allergy Development to an Accelerated Pathway to Tolerance (ADAPT) OIT program was a partnership with 10 major pediatric hospitals in five states across Australia to develop and implement the first standardized nationwide model of care for food allergy treatment.

The program was to enroll all infants presenting with a clinical history of an immunoglobulin E (IgE)-mediated allergic reaction to peanut before age 12 months and evidence of sensitization from a peanut skin prick test wheal of at least 3 mm or a peanut-specific IgE or Ara h 2-specific IgE of at least 0.35 kUA/L.

The 59 infants whose reaction to peanut had been anaphylaxis (Consortium for Food Allergy Research grade 3) could go straight to oral immunotherapy. Notably, 14 of the 29 patients in this group (48.3%) who had a threshold OFC did not react and were deemed tolerant to peanut.

Babies with an initial grade 1 to 2 reaction to peanut were to undergo OFC to peanut before commencing OIT both to confirm the diagnosis of peanut allergy and to determine peanut reaction threshold to inform the OIT starting dose. The OFC used a commercially available peanut flour (PB2).

Median age at OFC was 13 months, and it took a median 3 months from the time of initial reaction to the first allergy assessment in the allergy clinics.

Skin prick and blood test results were both significantly linked to a positive OFC (P<0.001) but did not predict the reaction threshold or severity.

#5848. US to install 36% more wind turbines in 2025 than previous year

The United States is expected to add more than 7 GW of wind installations in 2025, a 36% increase over the previous year, and the five-year outlook remains unchanged quarter-over-quarter from previous forecast, according to the “U.S. Wind Energy Monitor” report released by Wood Mackenzie and the American Clean Power Association (ACP).

Amid a challenging market environment, the report shows that the United States is on track to add 46 GW of new wind capacity from 2025 to 2029, with total projected volumes unchanged quarter-on-quarter from previous forecasts. However, timing has shifted, as 2026 and 2027 will deliver significant gains, at 10.7 GW and 12.7 GW, respectively, as more assets advance through the development pipeline.

While Q3 installations came in 23% below forecast at 932 MW, the market has shown progress with 3.8 GW queued for Q4 2025 — representing 52% of the year’s total expected capacity. This back-loaded installation pattern is consistent with typical project-commissioning timelines.

U.S. turbine order intake has rebounded to pre-One Big Beautiful Bill Act (OBBBA) levels quarter-over-quarter, supported by 2+ GW of firm commitments in Q3, the biggest intake in the region in the last nine months and a 79% quarter-over-quarter increase. However, true visibility remains limited as OEMs increasingly withhold project details and much qualifying “start-of-construction” activity occurs through off-site component manufacturing.

The market will then see a noticeable drop off, as 2029 weakens meaningfully quarter-over-quarter following project cancellations and inactive designations for late-decade capacity, driven by permitting and broader development challenges.

“The U.S. power market is facing mounting strain after a decade of flat demand, with utilities committing to 160 GW of large-load additions. This represents a significant opportunity for wind energy, which benefits from strengthened economic fundamentals and a compelling business case driven by its competitively low LCOE,” said Leila Garcia da Fonseca, director of research at Wood Mackenzie. “However, turbine costs remain elevated due to tariffs and mid-term wind growth will depend on resolving permitting and policy uncertainty.”

Power demand growth through 2029 is expected to average around 3% compared to just 0.7% over the previous decade, with data centers accounting for approximately 59 GW of the 90 GW total peak demand growth. This surge in baseload demand positions wind as a natural fit to meet rising power needs.

The five-year capacity outlook remains unchanged at 39.8 GW of added capacity quarter-over-quarter. The 2025-2027 pipeline is fully committed with all projects having turbine orders in place. More than 60% of the three-year capacity outlook has been commissioned or is under construction.

Activity is led by western states, such as Wyoming, New Mexico and others, that will account for 34% of activity in this time period. Major projects driving the outlook include Pattern’s 3.5-GW SunZia project in New Mexico, which will position the developer as 2026’s top installer, and Invenergy’s 998-MW Towner Energy Center in Colorado, the largest single project expected in 2027.

The market continues expanding geographically, with Arkansas bringing its first utility-scale onshore wind project online through Cordelio’s Crossover Wind.

The repowering market remains strong, as Wood Mackenzie projects that 18 projects will drive 2.5 GW of capacity additions in the next three years.

Wood Mackenzie expects the offshore installation pace to slow in Q4 2025 due to harsh winter weather conditions, pushing remaining capacity into 2026. Despite these near-term adjustments, Vineyard Wind has demonstrated strong execution, connecting 15 turbines in Q3 and delivering 200 GWh through nine months.

“U.S. offshore wind shows diverging momentum,” said Garcia Da Fonseca. “Projects under construction with COD estimated for 2026 continue to hit key milestones, but post-2027 developments face potential delays amid constrained wind turbine installation vessel capacity, driving delays and contract terminations.”

The offshore sector is also experiencing significant financial pressure.

The report highlights that uncertainty around tariffs is a threat to projections. Wood Mackenzie projects that tariffs will drive up turbine costs in 2026, before moderating in subsequent years. In total, U.S. onshore wind capex is projected to increase by 5% through 2029.

“U.S. wind turbine pricing is experiencing unprecedented uncertainty as conflicting market and regulatory forces interact,” said Garcia Da Fonseca. “Domestic manufacturing overcapacity relative to permitted project volumes, particularly after 2028, would normally place downward pressure on prices. Despite this, onshore wind costs are expected to continue rising due to tariff exposure on raw material inputs and subcomponents.”

#5846. Trump Is Gonna Cave On Offshore Wind In 5…4…3…

…JK! US President Donald Trump will never cry surrender in the war against offshore wind turbines. The President was burned once before, when a wind farm arose in Aberdeen Bay in Scotland, within view of a Trump-branded golf course back in the early 2000’s. Never again! The President has taken extreme measures to prevent such blight from tainting the shores of the United States. Nevertheless, scores of the pesky oversized pinwheels have already eluded the Trump chopper, and many more are on the way.

The latest news concerns CVOW, the 2.6-gigwatt Coastal Virginia Offshore Wind project under the wing of the leading utility Dominion. As the name of the project indicates, CVOW sits in the Atlantic Ocean about 24 nautical miles (28 land miles) off the coast of Virginia Beach, Virginia.

CVOW began taking shape during Trump’s first turn around the Oval Office, and construction was well under way when his second term began on January 20, 2025.

Immediately upon taking office, Trump abruptly suspended the offshore wind lease program administered by the Department of the Interior. He also ordered spurious re-reviews of offshore projects that were already in the permitting pipeline, and he had the Department of Justice administer a legally questionable buy-back program to prevent activity from stirring among other lease holders. In addition, he had the Interior Department issue multiple emergency orders aimed at stopping five offshore projects off the coasts of Rhode Island, Connecticut, New Jersey, New York, Maryland, and Massachusetts, where construction work was already well under way.

So far, though, only one part of the effort has stuck. Last year a federal judge affirmed that any President, Trump or not, has the authority to stop issuing new offshore leases. However, the same judge decided there is no blanket authority to suspend offshore leases that are already in the permitting process. The buy-back program is also in litigation, with critics raising questions about the funds used to pay off lease holders among other issues.

Additionally,  the Interior Department failed to convince multiple federal judges that the emergency orders had any merit. Work has continued on all five Atlantic coast projects, including CVOW.

CVOW began delivering its first kilowatts to shore in March, and Dominion recapped its progress on the wind farm in its Q3 report on October 30. As handily summarized by the news organization Maritime Executive, the project currently clocks in at 85% complete. All of the main turbine components — nacelles, towers, and blades — for the wind farm’s 176 offshore wind turbines have been fabricated. Forty-four have been fully installed so far. With a 45th coming any day now, the wind farm currently hosts 640 megawatts out of the 2,600 megawatt total.

Since Trump declared an “Energy Emergency” in January of 2025, it’s fair to ask why he has spent so much time, energy and taxpayer dollars to crush an entire domestic energy industry. After all, if one was not reading too closely between the lines of the declaration, the new energy policy is little more than a rehash of former President Barack Obama’s “All Of The Above” energy policy. As further embellished by Energy Secretary Chris Wright, the new version specifically taps multiple zero and low-emission energy resources for support including nuclear energy, biomass, hydropower, and geothermal energy, just like Obama did, along the emerging field of marine energy, which was barely a speck on the horizon while Obama was in office.

Energy storage, and the critical minerals needed in the clean tech industry, have also been gathered up in a Trumpian embrace.

Conspicuously absent, however, are the two most abundant, economical, and easily accessible domestic energy resources, namely, wind and solar.

If there really was an energy emergency…oh, never mind! Despite Trump’s complaints, offshore wind is a mature industry with a vigorous supply global supply chain and support equipment, as deftly illustrated by the CVOW project. In the October 30 report, Dominion noted that it takes only about two days for an offshore construction vessel to install a wind turbine on its foundation.

While the offshore wind construction timetable is subject to weather delays, Dominion also stated that the project is on schedule — despite any further delays related to last year’s stop-work order.

Speaking of the stop-work order, CVOW was conspicuously excluded from previous rounds of stop-work orders impacting the four other Atlantic coast wind farms under construction in 2025. If you’re guessing that Virginia’s Republican Governor, Glenn Youngkin, had a hand in that decision, drop a note in the discussion thread. Youngkin publicly supported the CVOW project but he was term-limited out of office last year. A stop-work order would have put an embarrassing crimp in his next-step political plans. The order came down only after Election Day 2025, after the Democratic candidate, Abigail Spanberger, won the post.

In a classic case of karma biting back, CVOW is a  more efficient and economical project than initially envisioned. A round of delays during Trump’s first term in office gave Dominion an opportunity to redesign the project with next-generation wind turbines. Those delays also enabled Dominion to take advantage of a new generation of turbine installation vessels that are purpose-built to cut offshore construction costs.

The results speak for themselves. In its October 30 report, Dominion indicated that CVOW costs were still consistent with its capital budget, even accounting for the cost of last year’s stop-work order and costs related to Trump’s tariff wars.

“The estimates on the levelized cost of energy (LCOE) also continue to fall,” Maritime Executive summarized. “After starting with a forecasted range of $80-$90 per MWh, and adjustments for changes after the change in administrations, they have lowered the LCOE to $62, down from an estimate of $83 presented in August” (LCOE is a calculation that provides a common ground for comparing costs among different forms of power generation).

Maritime Executive further reported that Dominion expects to save its ratepayers about $5 billion on fuel over the first 10 years of operation.

Trump’s war on wind has also petered out elsewhere. The Revolution Wind project off the coasts of Connecticut and Massachusetts has also been a target of  multiple stop-work orders over the past two years, with the latest hammer coming down just two weeks ago, when the 704-megawatt wind farm was almost complete.

Revolution Wind is now fully operational, joining the nearby Vineyard Wind project which also endured multiple attacks from Trump. As reported by public radio station WBUR, the savings from Revolution Wind is expected to ripple out through New England, saving $500 million for ratepayers in the region every year.

As for the domestic offshore wind industry writ large, the US lost thousands of onshore supply chain jobs all around the US in addition to job losses related to portside and offshore operation. However, the trade organization Oceantic Network is already prepping for a comeback. “The road to recovery for the embattled American offshore wind industry starts today with a new political mandate to tackle the affordability crisis,” Oceantic President and CEO Liz said in a public statement celebrating the Republican Party’s crushing defeat in the 202y midterm elections.

#5845. Hawaii Doctors May Soon Start Prescribing Fresh Food

— The federally funded initiative will start as soon as January

More than 100,000 Hawaii residents who qualify for Medicaid may soon find their doctors prescribing them fresh food as medicine.

The script could be for fresh fruit and vegetables, even ahi, beef, chicken, and eggs. The federally funded initiative will start as soon as January as part of a special state Medicaid program aimed at addressing chronic diet-related health issues in low-income communities.

The Food Is Medicine program could help many in Hawaii, where 1 in 3 households have limited access to safe, affordable, and nutritious food. It could also boost the local agricultural sector, as state advocacy and health groups have tailored the program to promote the use of local produce, which could inject millions of dollars into the economy and create almost 1,000 new jobs.

"It's really a no-brainer," said Alicia Higa, chief health equity officer at Waiʻanae Coast Comprehensive Health Center. "If there's an opportunity to give food as medicine to our people, we should absolutely be using that money to support the local farmers. We'll have an increased food supply, and we'll be much better off.... Not to mention it's the pono thing to do."

Conventional medicine has long turned a blind eye to the importance of nutrition, but its influence on health has been gaining greater attention with the uptick in obesity and diet-related illness globally. In Hawaii, where food insecurity and diet-related diseases are rife, advocates hope the move will help ensure lower income communities have sufficient food and that the food is nutritious and patients are well-versed in healthy eating.

Hawaii has long held goals to address its lack of a local food supply and winnowing population of farmers, but few programs have been able to meaningfully increase the islands' food security as it continues to be plagued by natural disasters.

Now Hawaii will join at least a dozen states in implementing the nutrition scheme, enabled by the Social Security Act's 11-15 waiver program, which allows for experimental and innovative health programs under Medicaid. The state's program will be rolled out in three phases, starting in January with nutritional education programs and prescription food boxes for eligible patients.

The program has been years in the making.

Healthcare providers and advocates recommend at least 15% of all produce and protein comes from local sources, setting it apart from other states. It's not binding, but it's an aspiration, said Jordan Smith of Hawaii Good Food Alliance, which is one of the program's lead agencies in the initiative. And it's still a work in progress.

"It's a lot of work to bring together a broken healthcare system and a broken food system, and asking them to work together," said Smith, the alliance's Food Is Medicine program manager.

Sourcing food from the continent is certainly an easier option, but healthcare providers are resolved to stay as local as possible. Otherwise, the food is mostly "coming across the ocean on a boat, it's not fresh, it's not necessarily culturally relevant," Smith said. "That's why we're exceptionally excited about the 11-15 waiver."

Big Island residents Moses and Suzette Paio have struggled with health issues associated with diet for years, making little progress in the past. What they could afford to eat plays a major role in their diet.

They're not alone, living on an island where 43% of residents report food insecurity. One-third of the state's households report insufficient access to adequate, nutritious, affordable food, according to Hawaii Food Bank's 2025 State of Food Security Report. And about half of Native Hawaiians and Pacific Islanders are food insecure, suffering the diet-related health ramifications.

Puna, where the Paios live, is classified as a food desert: a location with limited or no access to affordable, fresh, healthy, and nutritious food.

"It's not that I don't want to buy it," Suzette Paio said, "it's just that I can't."

The Paios took part in a pilot program that rolled out under the Medicaid waiver this year. It included access to five months of weekly produce and protein boxes, delivered by the Food Basket, Hawaii's food bank. The boxes included locally caught and harvested proteins, greens, and fruits.

Suzette Paio's average blood sugar has halved, something she has struggled to get under control for more than a decade. Moses Paio lost over 70 pounds.

Local bananas and papayas, "they're my candy," said Suzette Paio, having replaced cheaper sugary treats she used to enjoy.

The Paios have also started gardening, preserving food, and getting more active, taking lessons from other education programs.

"We just thank God for the opportunity that we had," Suzette Paio said, "because you know our health issues have been going on for a while."

Advocates are encouraged by the data they have been collecting during pilot studies, which have run for at least the past year, though there is much more research to do.

The University of Hawaii (UH), for one, is conducting a 5-year study on the program's influence on hypertension at various healthcare centers on the islands. UH assistant professor of nutrition Monica Esquivel, PhD, RDN, who is leading the study, says much more data will come as the program develops, but its premise is proof of a growing recognition of diet's influence on health.

In West Oʻahu, also considered a food desert, nutritionally focused healthcare programs have been operating since 2017, separate from the Medicaid initiative. The positive results kept them going, said Higa, who is also the CEO of ʻElepaio Social Services.

"We built it because we didn't have it," she said. "I think that's traditionally what Waiʻanae does because we're so far from everything."

During the COVID-19 pandemic, Waiʻanae Comprehensive Health Center tracked almost 500 Medicaid patients over 18 months, Higa said, when they received a $60 monthly produce prescription.

Higa's team tracked how much of the money was used, how the recipients' health changed, and how much it cost insurance. It resulted in about $118 in healthcare savings per patient, per month, she said.

Now, with the Med-QUEST program, the initiative has far greater security, Higa said.

Advocates believe the produce prescription will function like Hawaii's Da Bux program, which doubles the spending power of beneficiaries of the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program -- formerly known as food stamps -- when purchasing locally produced food.

There were almost 250,000 Da Bux transactions last year, accounting for more than $5.5 million in local produce, making it a triple win by benefiting the economy, the hungry, and local farmers.

Food Is Medicine could do the same, advocates say, given approximately 121,000 residents could be eligible for the program.

The initiatives could unlock $12.3 million in additional annual revenue for Hawaii farmers, according to a national Rockefeller Foundation analysis, the lion's share benefiting small and mid-sized farms. It could also boost the state's GDP by $125.5 million.

The results for farmers have already been seen on Oʻahu, with Waiʻanae Farmers Market vendors scaling up production in response to demand driven by food-based health programs run by Waiʻanae Comprehensive. The same has happened on the Big Island, with egg producers scaling up to meet demand, according to Food Basket CEO Kristen Frost Albrecht.

Micah Richards of Mauka Meats, a local meat provider, says his business and the ranchers he works with have benefited immensely. And he believes the program holds great promise for the entire agriculture sector.

Some hurdles exist, Richards said, including helping farmers and ranchers get food safety certifications so they can take part.

The greatest payoff from the program, he said, has been "having auntie come up to you at the market, tell you they feel better, they're making progress with their doctor, but all they feel they changed was going to the farmers market and having access to the funds for local meat and produce."

The Medicaid program's official rollout in January will start with prescriptions and nutritional education, but will mostly rely on organizations being able to deliver the service to eligible residents.

The second phase will include helping eligible Medicaid users stock their pantries and acquire cooking supplies, as well as phasing in medically tailored meals. The meals, on a national level, could help reduce the need for 2.6 million hospitalizations annually, a net cost savings of $23.7 billion, according to Tufts University.

The program is being coordinated by Med-QUEST, part of the state Department of Human Services, and the Hawaii Good Food Alliance. But the programs' full rollout will depend on individual health centers and food distributors, Med-QUEST Administrator Meredith Nichols said in an email, adding that the state is providing grants to help increase organizations' ability to deliver the programs statewide.

The prescriptions will give eligible recipients $50 per week to buy fresh protein and produce on Oʻahu, while other islands' residents will receive $55 weekly. The food could come in the form of food boxes, like the Paios get, or in vouchers to be used at farmers markets, like Waiʻanae Coast Comprehensive Health Center's patients do.

Advocates anticipate the program will be popular. On the Big Island, Moses Paio expounds the program's virtues openly, giving tips to friends, family, and members of his church. It's changed his life, he said, now that he's lost weight and can be more active.

"My yard pushes me. I see the grass growing," Moses Paio said. "There are times out there, I'm cutting grass, and I'm just crying. You know, I'm just thanking God that I can even just stand there."

#5841. America’s New Shipbuilding Orders Are Expensive Bets on Fossil Freight

South Korea’s Hanwha Group owns the Philadelphia shipyard that has become a centerpiece of Washington’s attempt to rebuild American commercial shipbuilding. Its Hanwha Ocean and Hanwha Systems subsidiaries acquired the US yard in December 2024. The investment creates and sustains American production capacity and jobs while transferring shipbuilding expertise, technology and training from South Korea to US workers. The facility is in America, but its corporate ownership remains South Korean. The company’s published orderbook, however, tells a more complicated story: two liquefied natural gas carriers, four firm orders for oil and chemical tankers, and options for another six tankers. Three LNG-fueled container ships ordered by Matson in 2022 predate the current administration. The newer LNG and tanker orders come from Hanwha’s own shipping affiliates. They can help restart production, but buying ships from another company in the same group does not demonstrate that independent shipowners will pay US construction prices.

The price gap is difficult to dismiss. Kinder Morgan’s January 2026 investor presentation estimates that a new medium-range Jones Act tanker would cost more than $240 million and require a long-term charter above $115,000 per day to justify construction. The existing charter market was around $90,000 per day. Kinder Morgan operates 16 tankers, with its fleet fully utilized, yet the gap between current charter revenue and the cost of a replacement vessel remains substantial. High utilization establishes a need for shipping services; it does not establish a financeable order for a new American-built tanker at today’s prices.

Coastal petroleum shipping also competes with other domestic infrastructure. A 2025 report to the Commodity Futures Trading Commission estimated moving gasoline from Houston to New York Harbor at under 8 cents per gallon by pipeline, about 20 cents by ship, and roughly 35 cents by rail. These illustrative route costs do not cover every destination, and tankers remain essential where pipelines are unavailable. They do show why expensive new tankers cannot count on charter customers accepting whatever price domestic construction requires. Longer term, the International Energy Agency estimates that electric vehicles displaced 1.7 million barrels of oil per day worldwide in 2025 and could displace about 5 million by 2030 under its policy scenarios. That does not mean US tanker demand vanishes, but fleet investment must account for changes in the cargo market over several decades.

LNG export carriers have a more plausible near-term growth market, although their prospects are different from the prospects of LNG-fueled container ships. US gas exports may expand, and LNG tankers will be needed to carry them. The commercial test for a US-built LNG carrier is whether it can win an arm’s-length contract against established Korean, Japanese and Chinese shipyards. Hanwha’s plan to train Philadelphia workers through its Korean shipyards can strengthen US industrial capability, and affiliated orders can provide an initial production run. The central uncertainty is whether independent buyers will still choose these ships once the group’s internal demand and any cargo preference are removed.

A broader domestic vessel market already exists. US-flag Great Lakes freighters carried 71.3 million tons in 2025, much of it iron ore, limestone, cement, coal and other bulk materials. Those cargo flows will change as steelmaking and energy systems evolve, while ferry services, harbour vessels, inland cargo craft and multipurpose ships will still require renewal. Battery-electric and hybrid-electric propulsion offer practical options on routes with manageable energy requirements and reliable charging access. Large, long-distance bulk ships need a more selective technology assessment, rather than an assumption that every vessel can run on batteries.

Recent projects demonstrate what a committed customer can contribute to ship economics. CMA CGM, Nike and Gemadept launched an electric inland barge in Vietnam for a 180-kilometre round trip. Nike agreed to fill 90% of its capacity for eight years, helping justify a vessel reportedly costing about twice as much as its diesel equivalent. A dedicated charging installation and renewable electricity form part of the service. That is a commercially structured freight proposition, with its higher capital cost supported by contracted utilization and expected operating savings.

Electric propulsion does not cure the American shipbuilding cost problem by itself. Washington State’s three new hybrid-electric ferries carry a $714.5 million shipbuilding contract, and the state’s estimate including additional equipment and other program expenses is approximately $1.15 billion. Construction has started; the ferries are not yet in service. The path to a productive shipbuilding industry still runs through standardized designs, modular fabrication, trained workers, repeat orders, reliable delivery and falling labor-hours per vessel. It would be a mistake to treat electrification as a substitute for manufacturing reform.

Hanwha’s South Korean capital and know-how could contribute to that reform by developing US suppliers and production skills that serve several vessel classes. That is a meaningful way to rebuild domestic capability even though the parent company remains foreign-owned. Its progress should ultimately be measured by independent repeat customers, improving construction costs and commercially competitive vessels, rather than affiliated orders or investment announcements. A US maritime strategy anchored to the fossil-fuel cargoes of today risks missing a growing opportunity to build modern domestic vessels for the freight, port and ferry services of tomorrow.

My TFIE Strategy Briefing assessment examines Hanwha’s orders, Kinder Morgan’s tanker economics and the market for repeatable electric and hybrid maritime construction. It follows my earlier analysis of the Jones Act’s shipbuilding capacity gap.

#5840. New Trials Back Quickly Approved Drugs for Primary Biliary Cholangitis

— Results show that biochemical normalization is a "feasible goal," researchers say

Treatment with both elafibranor (Iqirvo) and seladelpar (Livdelzi) led to alkaline phosphatase (ALP) normalization in the vast majority of patients with primary biliary cholangitis (PBC) who had elevated ALP levels after an incomplete response or intolerance to first-line therapy, two phase III trials showed.

Results from the ELSPIRE study showed that 85.3% of patients who received elafibranor achieved the primary endpoint of ALP normalization compared with 23.3% receiving placebo (P<0.0001) at week 52, reported Kris V. Kowdley, MD, of Liver Institute Northwest in Seattle.

The IDEAL trial demonstrated that 75.4% of patients treated with seladelpar achieved ALP normalization versus 16.1% of those receiving placebo (P<0.0001) at week 52, reported Cynthia Levy, MD, of the University of Miami Miller School of Medicine.

Results from both trials were presented at the American Association for the Study of Liver Diseases (AASLD) annual meeting in Denver, and the ELSPIRE study was also published in Hepatology.

Elafibranor is an oral dual peroxisome proliferator-activated receptor (PPAR) agonist that was granted accelerated approval for the treatment of PBC in adults based on results from the ELATIVE trial.

Meanwhile, the oral PPAR-delta agonist seladelpar was granted accelerated approval for the treatment of PBC in adults based on data from the RESPONSE trial.

"The key issue in our understanding of PBC, and where we are in PBC, is that it has become more and more clear that if you look at the best outcomes in patients that have PBC, it is in those that have achieved normal alkaline phosphatase," Kowdley told MedPage Today. "So, for a long time, we knew that alkaline phosphatase was a predictor of long-term outcomes."

The POISE trial defined biochemical response as the achievement of ALP under 1.67 times the upper limit of normal (ULN), with a reduction of at least 15% from baseline, and a normal total bilirubin level.

"Ever since then, all studies have used alkaline phosphatase of 1.67 above the upper limit of normal as the cutoff for predicting worse outcomes," Kowdley noted. "But, what about patients who have an elevated alkaline phosphatase above the upper limit of normal, but less than 1.67 times the upper limit of normal? That intermediate group ... also has an increased risk of adverse liver-related outcomes over the long term."

Thus, the ELSPIRE researchers sought to evaluate elafibranor in patients with PBC and an ALP over 1.00 but under 1.67 times the ULN after an incomplete response or intolerance to first-line therapy with ursodeoxycholic acid (UDCA).

"And as a proof of concept, [the study shows] you can achieve normalization in a very high proportion of patients if you start them earlier in the stage of the disease," Kowdley said.

ELSPIRE included 92 patients (median age 61 years, 92.4% women) who had a mean baseline ALP of 149.4 to 151.5 U/L. All patients had ALP over the ULN but under 1.67 times the ULN at randomization, and 96.7% had ongoing UDCA treatment for a median duration of around 5 years.

ALP normalization was considered to be less than or equal to the ULN (defined as ≤120 U/L at week 52) without the use of rescue therapy for PBC, and without experiencing a liver-related event or death due to any cause.

Patients were randomized 2:1 to elafibranor or placebo, and stratified into two categories by ALP (>1 to ≤1.33 times the ULN and >1.33 to <1.67 times the ULN).

Greater proportions of patients in both categories achieved the primary endpoint of ALP normalization with elafibranor versus placebo: 80.4% versus 26.1% in patients with ALP >1 to ≤1.33 times the ULN (P<0.0001), and 87.5% versus 14.3% in patients with ALP >1.33 to <1.67 times the ULN (P=0.0017).

Treatment-emergent adverse events (TEAEs) were observed in 79% of patients treated with elafibranor versus 70% treated with placebo.

Increased weight was reported in 22.6% of patients receiving elafibranor and 6.7% receiving placebo, with five TEAEs of increased weight considered to be related to elafibranor treatment.

Levy and colleagues (including Kowdley) found that higher response rates were observed at all timepoints with seladelpar, with the effect observed as early as a month into treatment, with 52.3% of seladelpar patients achieving ALP normalization at that time point versus 6.5% in the placebo group.

"These results help inform treatment decisions for an understudied population and demonstrate biochemical normalization as a feasible goal," Levy and colleagues concluded.

In IDEAL, 96 patients were randomized 2:1 to receive seladelpar or placebo for 12 months. Mean age was 61 years, 93.8% were women, and mean baseline ALP was 153 U/L.

Patients were considered responders if they achieved a 15% or more decrease in ALP levels from baseline, and if blood levels of the enzyme were ≤1.0 times the ULN.

Serious adverse events were reported in 3.1% of patients in the seladelpar group and 12.9% in the placebo group, with none deemed related to the drug.
