#5839. As Jackery Inventory Sells Out, Are Portable Batteries Set To Take Off?

I recently wrote reviews of the new Jackery HomePower 1000 Plus v2 and Explorer 100D. A few days later, a connection with Jackery messaged me that their Black Friday/Cyber Monday products had largely sold out. Just three days after launching on November 1. This includes 1000, 2000, 3600 and 5000 portable power and solar generator models. Additional models have sold out since then or will likely sell out soon. The recently launched Explorer 100D is still available in limited quantities at Walmart and Costco.

While Jackery will still take orders for Black Friday/Cyber Monday sales, most models currently listed for purchase will be on a preorder basis. Customers should check estimated delivery dates. Some restocking is expected in late November, although broader inventory availability may not recover until early next year.

While much of America was recovering from Halloween and election victory parties, portable batteries were selling out. This wasn’t the result of limited supply, but rather a massive, unanticipated increase in demand.

Between October 19th  and 26th, Jackery retail sales increased 755% at Costco, 106% at Walmart, 297% at The Home Depot and 442% at Lowes. For added perspective, at Costco alone, sales increased from 2379 to 20,343 over that one week.

Clearly, there have been climate-related disasters over the past year, including hurricanes and wildfires. Jackery’s collaboration with the Red Cross helps illustrate the benefits of portable power in emergency response. However, that only partially explains the growth. A related potential explanation is the growing push for household preparedness.  There are reports of at least 17 countries encouraging people to keep three to seven days of food, water and other essentials. Winter storm season, grid strain and rising energy costs could be stoking fears of potential power outages. The US FORTRESS America initiative has also added an emphasis on resilience. Together, these signals may be pushing “preparedness” beyond food and water to include power.

Preparedness is gaining emphasis with power becoming an increasingly important part of being prepared. The fear of “what if” can be a powerful motivator. Having backup power can keep the air handlers working for people’s furnaces. People on well water can keep the pumps running. Backup power can keep refrigerators full of food from spoiling.

Overall, Jackery is the global leader in solar generator sales volume and was named the “World’s No.1 Solar Generator Brand” by Frost & Sullivan. With over 15 years of experience and extensive safety protocols, the brand is well established. For the purchase of a product that manages risks, having a trusted brand is clearly valuable.

Although there has not been a detailed study of the consumer motivations, preparedness is likely a major motivator. However, versatile portable power stations have additional benefits. I keep finding new ways to use the HomePower 1000 Plus V2. And new possible benefits keep opening up.

Beyond providing emergency power, I can take power with me. I can set up an office remotely. I can run and recharge tools away from an outlet. I can power a radiant heater for a few hours while sitting outdoors. I can power an air conditioner for hours or run a fan all day. I can make coffee and cook food. In many ways, the batteries can replace functions once covered not just by a generator, but also a campfire or grill.

While using the battery, I also became more aware of my electricity usage. Seeing how quickly different appliances deplete the battery makes me realize where my utility bill is really going. Some things use less electricity than I anticipated, and some use far more. That awareness helps me to reduce my overall consumption.

And the UPS function can also save delicate equipment, as well as any work on computers and other machinery during a power disruption. I personally would not run a large print on my 3D printer without the backup battery. Providing stable power can extend the lifespan of many expensive devices.

The ability to integrate solar panels provides an additional level of preparedness, allowing the battery to be recharged by the sun when grid power is not available. However, solar can also charge the battery for daily use. While this may not yet be able to feed into the grid without additional equipment, people can reasonably use solar power fed into the battery to replace grid power at the point of use. When the regulations are figured out, balcony solar could expand the possibilities. All this can reduce people’s energy costs.

The battery can provide power when they need it, rather than just when the sun is shining. And when connected to the grid with a time of use (TOU) plan, it can charge when electricity is inexpensive and provide power when it is expensive. The savings from this alone could pay for the battery and start saving people money on their utility bills. And the grid becomes more stable in the process.

If the current battery capacity is not enough, Jackery makes expandible batteries to add more capacity.

In addition, the portable, scalable batteries can form the foundation of a whole home system. With greater utility communication, the added capacity could open up new possibilities for users to benefit while they help stabilize the grid. And they still benefit from the backup power. In addition, after seeing the capabilities, some people may even be inspired to look into going off-grid.

Of course, Jackery is likely not the only company seeing a surge in sales. I hope consumer demand and adoption is rising across the board. With a low barrier to entry and the ability to provide a level of preparedness, sales of portable batteries are likely to continue to grow.

Jackery is actively focused on removing the barriers to entry. Then the benefits of battery backup and portable power can be realized by more people. As more people see the benefits of portable expandable batteries, more people will want them. As more battery capacity is deployed, more applications can become viable. That not only has the ability to make homes more resilient, but also to build a more resilient grid. With the ability to shift consumption through distributed storage, more renewable energy can be utilized.

People who may have bought originally for preparedness will start to realize the broader benefits of their purchase. When people benefit from something, they will tend to rationalize it. This typically works better to change perspectives than trying to start with a rational argument. When people feel the relief of having backup power available for “what if,” they can then expand upon that with greater feelings of independence. Once they personally benefit from the storage that enables greater renewable adoption, they may increase their support for renewable energy. By addressing fears of “what if,” people may open themselves to thinking about “what’s possible.”

Of course, this might just be a temporary sales blip. But it could also be the start of a rapid expansion in home battery use. That could open up a wide range of new possibilities.

#5838. Smarter Cooling, Stronger Reliability: Advancing Wind Turbine Gearbox Performance

As the wind energy industry matures, operators and service providers are increasingly focused on maximizing turbine availability while controlling long-term maintenance costs. Although major drivetrain components often receive the spotlight, one overlooked system can have an outsized impact on turbine reliability and performance: gearbox oil cooling.

Heat exchangers play a critical role in maintaining proper oil temperature and viscosity within wind turbine gearboxes. When cooling systems become clogged with airborne debris, dust, or organic material, oil temperatures rise, lubrication performance declines, and component stress increases. Over time, these conditions can contribute to reduced gearbox efficiency, elevated maintenance demands, and avoidable downtime.

“Wind operators today are balancing increasing performance expectations with the realities of aging fleets and rising maintenance costs. Technologies that improve cooling efficiency and reduce service exposure can have a meaningful impact on long-term turbine reliability and operational profitability,” according to Mike Erickson, HYDAC’s Market Manager for the Wind Industry.

Traditional “panel cut” heat exchanger designs have long been susceptible to clogging due to their tightly packed fin structures. In many wind environments — particularly agricultural, dusty, or high-pollen regions — debris accumulation can severely restrict airflow. Oil leaks can further compound the issue by trapping contaminants within the exchanger core, making cleaning more difficult and labor intensive.

This operational challenge has driven the need for more resilient cooling technologies designed specifically for real-world wind farm conditions.

HYDAC’s new “Square Wave” heat exchanger design represents a significant advancement in addressing these reliability concerns. Engineered to allow debris to pass more freely through the exchanger fins, the design minimizes clogging while improving cooling efficiency under demanding operating conditions.

The importance of effective cooling cannot be overstated. Wind turbine gearbox oil typically operates within an optimal temperature range of approximately 45°C to 65°C. Even modest temperature increases can significantly impact oil viscosity. According to field data, a 12°C rise in oil temperature can reduce viscosity by nearly 28 percent — affecting lubrication quality and accelerating wear on critical drivetrain components.

Field trials have demonstrated measurable operational benefits from the Square Wave design. During a one-year trial on GE 1.x turbines, the upgraded exchanger consistently reduced clogging and lowered maintenance requirements compared to traditional panel cut cores. Operators reported reduced up-tower cleaning time and fewer temperature-related cooling faults.

Field validation across multiple turbine platforms has further reinforced the operational advantages of the Square Wave design. In one case study involving legacy 1 MW-class turbines operating in the Pacific Northwest, a major renewable energy operator installed pilot sets of Square Wave heat exchangers as part of a cooling performance evaluation. Installation teams reported the upgraded exchangers integrated seamlessly into the existing platform with no retrofit complications.

After initial operating data demonstrated improved cooling consistency, the operator expanded the evaluation program with additional units. Long-term SCADA analysis later showed turbines equipped with Square Wave technology operate approximately 20 to 25 percent cooler than comparable turbines using conventional heat exchanger designs under similar operating conditions. The data also highlighted another important advantage: the Square Wave cores continued to maintain airflow and cooling efficiency in debris-heavy environments where traditional exchanger designs became increasingly restricted over time.

The successful deployment also generated interest from additional wind service organizations seeking retrofit-ready cooling upgrades that could improve turbine reliability while reducing maintenance burdens across aging fleets.

“What operators are increasingly recognizing is that small improvements in thermal management can create meaningful gains in turbine reliability, maintenance efficiency, and long-term asset performance,” said Erickson. “The field data we’re seeing continues to validate the value of designing cooling systems specifically for real-world wind operating environments.”

More recently, long-term SCADA data from Mitsubishi platforms further validated the technology’s performance. After two years of operation, turbines equipped with Square Wave heat exchangers operated approximately 19 to 25 percent cooler than reference turbines using standard exchanger designs under comparable operating conditions.

For wind asset owners and service providers, the implications are substantial: Improved thermal management supports healthier oil viscosity, more stable gearbox operation, and potentially longer component life. At the same time, reduced cleaning frequency and fewer cooling-related service events translate directly into lower operational expenditures and increased turbine availability.

As the industry continues to prioritize lifecycle optimization and energy production efficiency, innovative subsystem upgrades such as advanced heat exchanger technology are becoming increasingly valuable. Rather than waiting for costly failures or performance degradation, operators are seeking practical retrofit solutions that improve reliability without requiring major system redesigns.

“Effective thermal management is critical to protecting gearbox health and maintaining oil performance over time. By addressing one of the most common causes of cooling degradation — debris accumulation — operators can improve uptime while reducing unnecessary maintenance interventions,” said HYDAC’s Erickson.

For wind stakeholders evaluating ways to improve gearbox reliability, reduce maintenance exposure, and enhance turbine performance, cooling system optimization deserves greater attention. Proven retrofit technologies like advanced heat exchanger designs can offer a practical path toward improved uptime and operational efficiency without requiring major system overhauls.

As fleets age and performance expectations continue to rise, collaboration between operators, service providers, and technology partners will be essential to building more resilient wind assets for the future. Now is the time to evaluate whether existing cooling systems are supporting — or limiting — long-term turbine reliability goals.

“HYDAC’s goal is to help wind owners and service providers solve practical operational challenges in ways that create long-term value across the entire asset lifecycle. Innovations like the Square Wave heat exchanger are designed to improve reliability, simplify maintenance, and support greater energy production over time.”

Don’t let cooling system limitations impact turbine performance.

Proactive cooling optimization can help operators reduce maintenance exposure, protect critical drivetrain components, and maximize energy production across the asset lifecycle. #5836. FDA Investigating Serious Malignancy Risk Linked to Gene Therapy

— Novartis acknowledges reports in SMA patients treated with Zolgensma

The FDA is investigating a serious risk of malignancy in patients treated with onasemnogene abeparvovec (Zolgensma) for spinal muscular atrophy (SMA), the agency said Friday.

The announcement came soon after drugmaker Novartis acknowledged that there were nine reports of tumors in patients who received the treatment. Two of the tumor cases were linked to the drug, the company said.

Zolgensma, an adeno-associated virus (AAV) vector-based gene therapy, was approved in 2019 to treat pediatric patients under 2 years of age with SMA and bi-allelic SMN1 mutations.

The FDA said it received confirmed reports of product-related insertional oncogenesis involving the glioma-associated oncogene homolog 1 (GL1) gene. GLI1 has the potential to cause cancer when overexpressed or abnormally activated.

The reports of neoplasia include tumors of the central and peripheral nervous systems, spinal or paraspinal regions, and kidney, the FDA said.

"Importantly, three cases involved tumors associated with the GLI1 oncogene," the agency noted. "In two of those cases, molecular analysis of tumor tissue demonstrated Zolgensma AAV vector DNA integration into the host genome, with the promoter region of the onasemnogene abeparvovec construct inserted upstream of or within the GLI1 oncogene." The mechanism of GLI1 overexpression in the third case is under investigation.

The FDA said the risk of neoplasia, including malignancy, applies to two onasemnogene abeparvovec products: Zolgensma, which is administered by intravenous infusion, and Itvisma, an intrathecal injection to treat adult and pediatric SMA patients ages 2 and older approved in 2025.

Both products contain the same vector and construct, the FDA said. To date, there have been no reports of neoplasia with Itvisma, the agency added.

"Since first approval in 2019, Novartis has received 9 reports of tumors in patients previously treated with Zolgensma," a Novartis spokesperson wrote in an email to MedPage Today.

"Of those, two cases to date have shown evidence of vector DNA integration into the DNA of the patients. In both cases, the patients underwent treatment and continue to be monitored," the spokesperson continued. "In each case, we timely and appropriately notified health authorities and will continue to work with them on next steps."

The spokesperson did not say when tumors may have developed in the other seven cases, or when they were identified.

SMA is caused by reduced levels of the survival motor neuron (SMN) protein due to deletions or mutations in the SMN1 gene. A nearly identical gene, SMN2, produces low levels of functional SMN protein.

Onasemnogene abeparvovec uses an AAV vector to replace the SMN1 gene. Its prescribing information notes a theoretical risk of tumorigenicity from the integration of AAV vector DNA into the genome.

"The potential risk of tumors due to vector integration is currently included in the Zolgensma prescribing information," Novartis said.

Advocates recently raised concerns on social media after learning from their doctors that Novartis had received reports of tumors in patients treated with the gene therapy. SMA Europe, an umbrella organization of SMA patient groups in Europe, acknowledged the reports in a news release early Thursday.

"We understand that the relevant regulatory authorities are actively involved and are currently assessing the available evidence and determining what further steps may be needed," SMA Europe stated. "We trust in the regulatory processes established to evaluate safety signals and to take the necessary measures to protect patients and ensure the continued safety of medicines on the market."

In the U.S., the Muscular Dystrophy Association (MDA) said it was "seeking additional information, reviewing the available scientific and safety data with clinical and research experts, and has reached out to Novartis."

The MDA added that "limited information is available currently about the timing of events, nature of the tumors, and any future monitoring of treated individuals that may become appropriate."

A 2023 case report described a 16-month-old boy with SMA who was diagnosed with an epithelioid neoplasm of the spinal cord 14 months after receiving onasemnogene abeparvovec; the finding was considered inconclusive. A 2025 case report detailed a pilocytic astrocytoma in a child with SMA treated with onasemnogene abeparvovec; a molecular analysis suggested tumorigenesis was causally independent of the gene therapy.

Earlier this year, researchers identified vector integration in a brain tumor in a 5-year-old boy with severe mucopolysaccharidosis type I (Hurler syndrome) who received another AAV gene therapy, describing the case in the New England Journal of Medicine. A correspondence last month described an integration-associated paraspinal neoplasm after AAV gene therapy in a 3-year-old boy with Krabbe disease.

More than 6,000 patients have been treated with Zolgensma in clinical trials, managed access programs, and commercial treatment, Novartis said.

The tumor reports are not the first controversy involving Zolgensma. Soon after the therapy was approved, the FDA criticized the Novartis AveXis unit over data manipulation that affected the accuracy of animal product-testing results.

#5835. Solar and storage companies voice support for federal permitting reform

Hundreds of solar and storage companies have co-signed a letter addressed to Congress in support of the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act of 2026 (BAAJA) (S. 5653).

“You can’t lower energy costs if you can’t build the energy projects, and these companies know that this bipartisan legislation will help get America building again,” said Tim Pawlenty, CEO of the Solar Energy Industries Association (SEIA), in a press release.

BAAJA was introduced in the Senate on Sept. 30 by Sen. Shelly Moore Capito (R-WV), and co-sponsored by Sen. Mike Lee (R-UT), Sen. Sheldon Whitehouse (D-RI) and Sen. Martin Heinrich (D-NM). The legislation is focused on quickening permitting for a range of projects with federal oversight, many of them related to energy production. BAAJA specifically calls out solar photovoltaic systems, energy storage and on- and offshore wind, but also includes language for fossil fuel sources, such as natural gas, oil and coal.

If passed, the Senate bill would amend sections of the National Environmental Policy Act, Clean Water Act and Endangered Species Act of 1973 with the goal of shortening project permitting windows. According to the text, it would change and reduce which projects would need to be reviewed under those acts, such as water quality certifications; shorten the length of review periods for projects; and would not require permits for oil and gas drilling on land not owned by the federal government.

BAAJA would also grant the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission the ability to issue permits for some electricity transmission projects.

According to a SEIA analysis, if BAAJA was passed, solar energy output could increase by 167 GW between 2028 and 2035. The companies that signed this letter to Congress believe that federal permitting practices are outdated, and permitting reform is a solution to lowering energy costs.

“The message from more than 300 companies comes as voters made clear in the midterm elections that lowering energy costs is a top concern,” the group stated in a press release. “Permitting reform is urgently needed to meet rising demand and get more reliable, affordable solar and storage projects built.”

BAAJA is currently under review by the Committee on Energy and Natural Resources.

#5834. Alas, Poor Cybertruck, We Hardly Knew Thee

If you felt a ripple in the space-time continuum yesterday, yes, the rumors are true. All too sadly true. The Tesla Cybertruck, introduced to motorists in 2019 with great fanfare and a sales goal of up to 250,000 units per year, is slated to cross the rainbow bridge into the dustbine of automotive history sometime next year. Not to worry, Tesla fans, rumor has it that Tesla’s Cybercab robotaxi will pick up where the Cybertruck left off — oh, wait. Hold, please…

Tesla is notoriously shy about releasing sales figures, but there are ways to reach an approximation. Earlier this year CleanTechnica calculated that the Cybertruck barely scraped by 2025 with just 17,012 units delivered. Even so, just one year earlier Tesla CEO Elon Musk was still pitching the 250,000 Cybertrucks-per-year goal.

Even though it is soon to be gone, the Cybertruck will never be forgotten. Much in the same way as the Edsel, “Cybertruck” will linger on as shorthand for a fabulously hyped product without an audience.

The Cybertruck was promised as a full sized, five-seat electric pickup truck with ample storage room. Tesla delivered on the zero emission angle, of course, and the five seats, too. However, the automaker failed to deliver on pickup truckyness in any substantive way (see entire CleanTechnica archive here).

So … don’t let the door hit you on the way out. Multiple electric pickup trucks are taking up the space left by the Cybertruck, including the forthcoming Ford Fathom alongside offerings from Rivian, Slate Auto, and other automakers.

Elon Musk himself announced the untimely death of the Cybertruck in a post on his social media site X earlier today.

“Tesla will be winding down production of the Cybertruck at Gigafactory Texas around the middle of next year to make room for increased Cybercab production,” Musk stated somewhat blandly, perhaps expecting his audience to appreciate the good news about “increased Cybercab production.”

If so, Musk was probably disappointed to hear from X users like Ben McCombe, who skipped over the implication that the Cybercap would occupy more space in the Tesla Gigafactory in Austin, Texas. Instead, he zeroed in on the Cybertruck in a particularly pithy comment:

“Installed tooling to build 125k Cybertrucks a year.

“Made just $100m in gross profits from sales.

Tesla’s stock tanked on November 3 and the following two days, after Democratic candidates dominated the all-important mid-term elections in both Houses of Congress, and in statehouses across the country, including Tesla’s home state, Texas. The power shift all but guarantees a more vigorous application of federal and state regulations governing Tesla’s products and operations.

Still, the automaker scored a partial recovery just a few days later. Tesla stock was swinging upwards as of midday on November 6, with Musk’s Cybercab announcement possibly factored into the partial recovery. However, those incoming lawmakers are going to be taking a close look at the Cybercab, and so far the picture is not pretty.

One sign of trouble emerged on September 3, when Musk failed to appear at a long-anticipated Cybercab launch event in Texas. The very next day, the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration went out of its way to let everyone know that it is investigating Tesla’s self-certification for the Cybercab under the National Traffic and Motor Vehicle Safety Act.

“The US Department of Transportation’s National Highway Traffic Safety Administration (NHTSA) today announced that it has opened an Audit Query (AQ) to investigate Tesla’s certification that its new Cybercab meets all applicable Federal Motor Vehicle Safety Standards (FMVSS),” NHTSA announced on September 4.

NHTSA initially gave Tesla until September 30 to respond to a list of 21 questions about the Cybercab self-certification, then extended the deadline to October 30.

Anyone eager to learn how automakers go about self-certifying new models under the National Traffic and Motor Vehicle Safety Act will be sorely disappointed, unless they are privileged to read the documents Tesla finally submitted. “The tricky part is that in its public response, Tesla offered one whole sentence. ‘The entirety of this file is confidential business information,'” Carscoops reported earlier today.

So close and yet so far. While the Cybercab investigation is still bubbling away on the backburner, Tesla has also set itself up for a whole ‘nother round of investigations related to its newly unveiled “flying car,” part of a suite of high-end sports cars modeled after the original Tesla Roadster.

The Roadster reboot was slightly clouded by the release of a new documentary on Elon Musk’s rise to both automotive and political power, but just slightly. The automotive press went nuts over the spectacle of the new Tesla Roadster rocket going airborne for a few seconds, then safely landing on all four tires with an assist from SpaceX-designed thrusters.

Whether or not that actually counts as a flight or just a thruster-enhanced jump, the Federal Aviation Administration has already stated that the rocket does not meet its definition of an aircraft.

As of for the question of whether or not the vehicle can be used on public roads, that’s something for the NTHSA to weigh in on. On Tesla’s part, though, the automaker has reportedly stated that the rocket is not designed for use on public roads. That seems to cut NTHSA out of the picture, though some industry observers have suggested that the agency could adopt a framework that encompasses vehicles with thrusters.

Musk himself has suggested that anyone who purchases the thruster-equipped Roadster can make it fly on a purpose-built tack on Tesla (or perhaps SpaceX) property, presumably in Texas.

The land use issue opens up a whole ‘nother can of worms regarding Musk’s operations in Texas. If anything, the offer of an off-road rocket track seems to let Tesla off the hook for the actions of any rambunctious rocket driver who insists on trialing the car on public roads.

For the record, Musk the movie opened initially in Los Angeles and New York City on October 9. A wide release on hundreds of screens was scheduled for October 16, but the film’s distributor, Bleecker Street, abruptly pulled back on the plan under new ownership. On October 27, representatives for the film contacted CleanTechnica to clarify that the Musk documentary was still showing on scores of screens around the country even after the dial-down. Either way, if you missed it in theaters, you can catch the whole thing — including the Cybertruck debacle and so much more — streaming as of today, November 6, on Amazon Prime Video, iTunes, and YouTube along with cable services.

This town hall is a critical first step toward demanding a just, affordable, and clean energy future for everyone in Tampa Bay.”

“Tampa residents have been struggling under the weight of skyrocketing electricity bills, all while Tampa Electric walks away with record profits year after year and passes the costs of fuel, storm recovery, and even its brand new Midtown headquarters onto ratepayers,” said Isabella Moeller, Florida Organizer for Food & Water. “But our community has had enough. TECO is a for-profit company beholden to shareholders only, that’s why we’re making a wide call to our local elected officials to hold TECO and its regulators accountable to the people they serve. With the incoming Democratic Congress that actually trusts science and wants to eliminate measles once and for all, Kennedy's impeachment may be the only way out of this mess."

Kennedy's perceived lack of action on the measles epidemic, along with his questioning the safety and effectiveness of vaccines, has angered many public health advocates. His running of HHS itself, including closing down several offices and redirecting the way appropriated funds were spent -- for example, keeping the Agency for Healthcare Research and Quality open but taking away most of its funding and rendering it inoperable -- also has drawn controversy.

If Kennedy doesn't decide to leave of his own accord, as Cabinet secretaries sometimes do halfway through an administration, "he's going to be on the hot seat a lot," Georges Benjamin, MD, CEO of the American Public Health Association, said in a phone interview. "Every time he does one of these illegal or immoral acts that he's continued to do over time, or says something that is ill-tempered or inappropriate ... I expect that in addition to groups like mine calling him out, he'll be called out more and more by Congress. So I think he's going to be miserable in terms of the oversight that he's going to see."

Indeed, future members of Congress have already begun talking about investigating Kennedy. Democrat Abdul El-Sayed, MD, the senator-elect from Michigan, told CNN that he was going to look into Kennedy's cuts to the FDA and CDC and how they affected the explosive diarrhea outbreak this summer that was traced to tainted lettuce.

"This is not about retribution for something past," El-Sayed told CNN. "This is about understanding what happened, holding people accountable for what they did, and then solving the problem moving forward."

The question becomes how long Kennedy will be willing to put up with the increased scrutiny, Georges said. "Obviously my dream is he's fired or quits. Is it possible they might try to impeach him? It's possible, but you've got to get a two-thirds vote [in the Senate] to do that, and whether you can get enough Republicans to come on board, I don't know."

Kennedy appears to have some administration support, at least for now. A story in Politico Thursday noted that "Emily Hilliard, senior press secretary at Kennedy's Health Department, said Kennedy 'will continue delivering President Trump's Make America Healthy Again [MAHA] agenda and advancing historic policies that put the health of the American people first.'" In an emailed statement, she said the administration "has transformed federal food and nutrition policy ... and reshaped the federal approach to scientific research and environmental health."

And Tony Lyons, who works for a number of organizations in the MAHA movement that Kennedy is aligned with, said he'd work with congressional Democrats who were open to Kennedy's plans related to things MAHA cares about.

To move forward, "we partner with absolutely everyone who's willing to partner with us -- companies who will listen, politicians who will work with us from any party, activists, influencers, MAHA moms in every corner of the country," Lyons said during a virtual call with supporters, according to The Hill.

Policy analyst Steven Grossman, JD, a former HHS official, said in a MedPage Today opinion piece Friday that although he had been thinking Kennedy would stay for the whole administration, that's no longer as likely. "Post-election, the job will quickly become a nightmare for Kennedy, as he will have to respond to hostile investigative hearings led by Democrats on the health committees. And Kennedy is unlikely to get White House help: Trump will have bigger fights to address and less political capital to spend."

"Also, if impeachment hearings were to start, Kennedy would be behind only Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth as the object of Congressional attention," he added. "This situation will evolve, but I suspect Kennedy will leave (resign) rather than face congressional challenges to his own hubris."

Michael Baker, director of healthcare policy at the American Action Forum, said in an email that although Kennedy's fate at the moment is unclear, "there are both new and returning members [of Congress] that want to focus on various parts of the healthcare ecosystem. And I expect oversight of the Department of Health and Human Services and its leadership to be a top priority in that focus."

"From the most-favored-nation drug price agreements to the changes in the ACIP [Advisory Committee on Immunization Practices] and pediatric vaccine schedule to the Medicaid cuts, there is no shortage of policies that congressional committees will investigate, and I think that oversight effort happens no matter who is sitting in the secretary's (or any other official's) chair," he said.

#5830. Well, Someone 3D-Printed A Whole Engine And It Actually Ran (Sort Of)

You've probably sat around a campfire at some point in your life and figured out firsthand that plastic and heat don't mix. Whether you threw an empty soda bottle or marshmallow bag in and watched it shrivel up, or propped your sandals up on the stones around the fire and witnessed your soles melting, you get it.

Plastic is a pretty good insulator, but it has a pretty low melting point. ABS has a melting point of around 440 degrees Fahrenheit, while most available PLAs melt at 340-ish degrees. If you've spent any time looking at your engine's oil or coolant temperature gauges, you'll know that a running engine is pretty stable in the low 200-degree range, but the combustion chamber can get up to 2,500 degrees during the peak of the power stroke. Plastic doesn't stand a chance, which is why most engines are crafted from cast iron or aluminum.

We've already seen what happens when you try to use a 3D-printed cylinder head; the results aren't pretty. With the kind of heat an engine sees, plastic just isn't the preferred material to work with. There are certainly some engines that have made extensive use of plastic, including the Torlon-based engines from Polimotor Research in the 1970s and 80s, but there isn't a high-enough-heat plastic to manage combustion chamber heat spikes, so a blend of metal and plastic is necessary.

YouTuber and mad scientist Alexander's Laboratory recently built and ran a pair of 3D-printed plastic engines, a single-cylinder and a parallel twin. We'll talk through both engines and their unique challenges in a second. First, we should take a step back and think about the implications of potentially building real working 3D-printed engines as prices come down and the technology both improves and becomes commonplace.

Have you ever built (or rebuilt) an engine for one of your project cars? There are just so many pieces and parts you have to buy, and there's so much measuring and clearance-checking to be done before the parts can all get bolted together. It's time-consuming and expensive, but the longest time you'll spend working on it is the shipping time to get all of the parts. Imagine if, someday, every engine in every car shared interchangeable components that could be stocked at any local auto parts store, and the rest could be 3D-printed at home. Wouldn't that be cool?

There are certainly still components that would need to be made out of metal, of course. The obvious first step would be to use metal for the combustion chamber, cylinder head, pistons, and crankshaft. You would also need to figure out a bearing system that works for the crankshaft and camshafts. Then there are things like the valves, valve springs, hardware, water pump components, and the accessory drive pullies.

Alexander is able to make most of his engines out of plastic, including the water pump and drive gears, but I'd go with metal for those on a full-scale engine, purely for longevity's sake. In the end, if you could make it work, you would have an engine significantly lighter than a comparable aluminum cylinder head and engine block unit. Recent research indicates swapping from a metal component to a 3D-printed plastic replacement cuts weight by 30% and costs by 15%. With enough research, you could add structural lattice inside some areas of components to make it even lighter, or allow better coolant flow to critical heat spots. Now this is exciting!

If you wanted to build a 3D-printed plastic engine, what steps would you need to take so it would run for more than a few seconds? As mentioned above, some metal is needed to keep it alive. Alexander strategically used machined steel for both the cylinder walls and the combustion chamber surface. This is smart, as it allows a sealing surface for the metal valves and the ability to thread in a common spark plug. The crankshaft is also metal, as is the surface of the pistons, but pretty much everything else comes straight off the printer.

In the single-cylinder-engine video above, Alexander had some issues with sparks and grounding. It's harder to get everything to ground out properly when the engine is non-conductive, of course. Once it gets running, though, it sure sounds like a pretty normal single-cylinder four-stroke engine, the kind you might find in a lawnmower or go-kart. After getting everything dialed in, Alexander piles on the throttle until the engine decides to eat itself. We don't get an indication of how long it ran, but eventually the carbon-reinforced plastic connecting rod gives up the ghost and shoots through the side of the plastic block.

Trying again with a more balanced twin-cylinder engine, Alexander might actually be on to something. Using some beefed-up components, a little more metal, and better heat management, this little 250-cc twin seems, in the video anyway, to run and work as a standard small motorcycle or scooter engine would. With a better-built engine and more care taken in its running, the twin just keeps on chugging. Maybe it's time to start developing open-source plastic engines that can run with just a few off-the-shelf components. It could be cool.

#5829. Study Finds Evidence of Cannabis Use 2,800 Years Ago

— Findings point to consumption at least 300 years earlier than previously known use

People may have been getting high off cannabis earlier than previously thought -- at least 2,800 years ago, a new study suggests.

Archaeologists who led a dig at a monumental tomb in Siberia said they turned up evidence of the earliest known use of cannabis for psychoactive purposes.

The findings point to cannabis consumption at least 300 years earlier than previously known use in neighboring China.

Ancient drug use has long intrigued scholars. The Greek historian Herodotus wrote about inhabitants of Central Asia smoking cannabis around 440 B.C., and recent archaeologists have found the seeds in tombs across its highlands.

The team from Germany, Russia, Sweden, and Switzerland said analysis of hair in the royal tomb where cannabis seeds turned up sheds new light on the plant's role in ancient societies.

"It's extremely rare that we have both preserved plant parts and human soft tissue with the active compounds in it in the same context," said study author Gino Caspari, PhD, MSc, an archaeologist at the University of Bern.

It's not clear whether the cannabis was consumed through inhalation or ingestion, he said.

The dig took place starting in 2017 at a large burial mound at the Tunnug 1 site in the Uyuk Valley of southern Siberia, home to one of the earliest monumental tombs showing material culture of the Scythians -- ancient nomads who migrated from Central Asia to southern Russia and Ukraine.

The team, deployed "essentially out in the middle of nowhere," lived in tents for months and faced a spring-to-autumn season that variously featured swamps, snowstorms, frosts, and swarms of mosquitoes. Herds of horses ran freely across the grassy steppe.

Larger artifacts on the site include weapons in the burials, horse gear, and animal-style motifs. But the team "struck gold" as it also found tiny black spots that turned out to be cannabis seeds along with preserved human hair, Caspari said.

"It's only so often as an archaeologist that you do get to drug test a person that's been dead for almost 3,000 years," he said.

Radiocarbon dating on some of the more than 1,000 seeds helped establish the time of origin, and "they are not there by accident" but deposited within the tomb, suggesting that the plant material had significance in the community, he said.

Results were published in the journal Science.

Not all independent experts were convinced.

The hair analysis "is scientifically weak" and there's not enough evidence to tell whether cannabis was used, wrote Volker Auwaerter, PhD, head of the forensic toxicology section at the University Medical Center in Freiburg, Germany, in an email.

"For a central part of the study, the article falls far short of what would have been possible," Auwaerter said. "This matters because the hair data carry the abstract's main claims (cannabis consumption and use for its psychoactive properties)."

Today, scholars don't consider ancient accounts trustworthy without corroborating evidence. Because the cannabis plant has other uses -- seeds are pressed for oil and fibers used for cloth -- their presence alone doesn't confirm drug use.

Auwaerter, who was not part of the study, said the data didn't distinguish consumption from external exposure -- in other words, the hair could have picked up traces of weed simply by being buried together with it. He said a lab test involving forensic toxicology expertise would have been advisable and easy to arrange.

But Elisa Guerra Doce, PhD, of the University of Valladolid in Spain, who has written about use of consciousness-altering substances in European prehistory, said toxicological hair analysis was not new in archaeology and has been used to identify consumption of psychoactive substances. She was not involved in the study.

In an email, she credited the authors for showing, through their methodology, that "cannabis was not merely deposited as a funerary offering but was actually consumed by individuals associated with the burial rite."

#5828. NRDC Assessment of BAAJA, the 2026 Permitting & Transmission Bill

The Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act of 2026 (BAAJA) is the result of years of negotiations on permitting reform. The product is a bill that combines critically important transmission and grid reforms with significant and concerning changes to federal environmental laws, permitting standards, and judicial remedies.

The transmission provisions in the bill would produce substantial and durable benefits, updating an aging power grid by allowing new investments. These reforms, which NRDC has long supported, are an essential component of accelerating the electrification and decarbonization of the power sector and achieving greenhouse gas reduction targets. On their own, these changes are much needed and overdue; they would also help any future clean energy incentives and standards succeed in cutting emissions. But transmission is an enabling technology rather than a substitute for policies that directly drive clean energy investment and reduce pollution.

However, there are a number of concerning provisions that raise substantial issues and reinforce the position of incumbent energy interests. The “project certainty” language is designed to ensure projects cannot be arbitrarily canceled. As drafted, it could benefit fossil fuel, mining, data center, and other industrial projects more than clean energy. It could also limit agencies’ ability to address newly discovered harms, constrain future pollution regulation, and create large taxpayer-funded corporate handouts.

The bill would also weaken key elements of core environmental laws, including the Clean Water Act (CWA), the Endangered Species Act, the National Environmental Policy Act (NEPA), and the National Historic Preservation Act (NHPA). The bill would narrow environmental review across those statutes, diminish state and Tribal authority, constrain public participation, and restrict courts’ ability to stop projects proceeding under unlawful permits. These changes erode fundamental protections for communities.

The backdrop, of course, is the Trump administration’s nonstop attacks on clean energy projects, tax incentives for clean energy, and climate standards. NRDC’s analysis finds in aggregate that the Trump administration’s actions could double carbon emissions from the power sector over the next decade while raising consumers’ electric utility bills by $30 billion per year by 2035. Lawmakers should push for tangible evidence that this has changed before voting on the legislation.

While NRDC is encouraged by the transmission provisions, other elements of the bill are deeply flawed. We will be seeking improvements in the coming weeks and will take a position on the bill before a floor vote.

Below is an assessment of the most positive and most negative elements of the bill. This is not intended to be comprehensive.

An aging power grid desperately needs updating, and with more extreme weather and surging demand from data centers, getting new electricity connected to the grid quickly is essential to keeping energy costs down and maintaining resilience. In one fell swoop, this legislation would address these issues, producing the necessary conditions to deploy more clean energy.

This legislation would provide a dramatic near-term boost to the nation’s grid by increasing both the amount of power that existing transmission lines can carry and the supply of electricity available to meet growing demand. It establishes procedures that could cut the time to build a major new transmission line to five to six years from 10 years—or sometimes significantly longer—today.

The Midwest’s multi-value projects: How agreeing on who pays can unlock transmission

In 2011, the Midwest grid operator, MISO, approved 17 high-voltage lines costing more than $5 billion and spread the cost across the region based on who benefits. Within about a decade, 16 of the 17 were in service, helping to connect wind power across the Midwest.

Between regions, where no such agreement exists, almost no major lines were approved in the decade after FERC’s 2011 planning rule. The bill tries to bring the Midwest’s approach to lines that cross between regions.

In the short term, it would require utilities to upgrade existing transmission lines and deploy advanced transmission technologies whenever their benefits exceed their costs. This technology can increase the capacity and efficiency of existing transmission lines, reduce congestion, and improve reliability, often at a cost that is 5 to 10 times cheaper than building new transmission. If deployed aggressively in the short term, this could free up more than 100 gigawatts of transmission capacity—enough to power 75 million homes.

Importantly, the bill goes beyond simply requiring utilities to consider these technologies: It directs the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission (FERC) to establish timelines for deployment, makes it easier for utilities to recover their costs, and establishes penalties for utilities that fail to deploy cost-effective technologies.

From PJM’s queue freeze to Southwest Power Pool’s fix

In 2022, PJM, which runs the grid for 13 states and Washington, D.C., stopped taking new requests to connect to the grid while it worked through a backlog of more than 300 gigawatts, 95 percent of it renewables and storage. It didn’t reopen until April 2026, so projects that applied after 2022 are only now starting their studies.

In March 2026, FERC approved a new approach from Southwest Power Pool, which runs the grid across much of the central United States. It plans transmission and new power plants together over 20 years, charges developers a standard up-front fee to connect, and studies projects once a year with a single decision point. The bill would require every region to adopt a process like this within two years and to speed up studies with better data and automation.

The bill makes major interstate power lines easier to build by strengthening federal authority over large interstate transmission lines. Currently, a state can block or indefinitely delay a project that would provide broad regional or national benefits. If a state rejects an eligible project or fails to act within one year, the bill requires FERC to issue a permit for a covered transmission line when a developer seeks federal review and the project satisfies specific criteria. FERC must then spread the costs fairly among all consumers who benefit from the projects.

The bill also requires neighboring grid regions to plan interregional transmission jointly, assess the benefits of potential projects, and establish methods for allocating costs. Despite a FERC order issued in 2011 that was meant to spur these cross-regional power lines, currently, virtually no major lines have been built between regions because there is no durable process for planning them or determining who should pay. The bill addresses this long-standing problem and codifies important elements of FERC’s updated regional planning framework from 2024, known as Order 1920.

The bill will also reduce the long wait times for energy projects to connect to the grid. Approximately 2,000 gigawatts of proposed generation and storage are waiting to connect to the grid, and 85 percent of that capacity is solar, wind, or storage. Projects often wait years for studies and may receive unexpectedly high upgrade costs late in the process. The bill encourages more coordinated planning, provides developers earlier information about costs, and improves data and automation.

Taken together, these transmission and interconnection reforms are a once-in-a-generation opportunity that would produce significant and durable benefits. The reforms would also facilitate the infrastructure needed so that future clean energy incentives and standards could succeed.

The data center provisions could provide protection for existing utility customers and support grid investments by requiring data centers to pay for their impact to the grid. It would direct FERC to develop pricing rules designed to prevent transmission costs created by data centers (generally 20 megawatts or more) from being shifted to other ratepayers and ensure data centers provide financial assurance to avoid costs shifting in the future. FERC would also have to revise transmission pricing policies and require standardized analysis of upgrades and cost-reduction options. These provisions address the transmission portion of the broader effects of rapid data center growth. The bill does not address local air pollution, water consumption, noise, land use, reliance on on-site fossil fuel generation, transparency, or public participation.

With geothermal energy poised to be a major player in the clean energy future, the bill provides policy reforms that could increase permitting efficiency and lower some of the barriers to geothermal development. But the geothermal provisions also come with their drawbacks, including the expansion of Section 390’s oil and gas activity categorical exclusion to geothermal development, which allows for significant drilling and production activities to take place on public lands without environmental review.

In an effort to respond to the Trump administration’s relentless attacks on wind and solar projects, this legislation includes “project certainty” language to protect developers from unreasonable attacks. Unfortunately, these provisions could have problematic unintended consequences, including locking in the Trump administration’s preferential treatment of oil, gas, data centers, and mining projects. This part of the legislation could also lead to a slew of industry lawsuits that result in taxpayers paying billions of dollars to private industry.

These “project certainty” provisions would largely prevent federal agencies from canceling, suspending, or changing federal approvals once issued. The provision’s reach is not limited to energy projects and is not limited to specific agencies or types of permits. The legislation sets out a small handful of circumstances in which agencies can modify an issued permit. Notably, while these circumstances include national security or defense concerns, they do not include environmental harm—even if newly discovered, severe, or widespread. Its broad language could even lead to industry arguments and legal claims that operating facilities are protected from subsequently adopted pollution requirements under the Clean Air Act and other statutes. State permits to implement future U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) standards for power plant carbon emissions, for example, could face legal challenges based on this provision.

And if a project is canceled or amended, a company can go to court to get its permit reinstated—as well as require the government to pay for its litigation expenses and the cost of project delays. The government could also be forced to use taxpayer money to make an additional payment of 25–50 percent of total project costs incurred to the company. For a single large energy project, this could easily amount to hundreds of millions, or even billions, of dollars.

A separate provision would allow energy-project developers to sue agencies for alleged “disparate treatment.” The approach uses a five-year comparison period that could embed the second Trump administration’s energy preferences in the legal baseline, and thus advantage oil, gas, and coal projects. And it prevents agencies acting in good faith from fully defending themselves in court. Successful claims could result in payments equal to 50–100 percent of projected construction costs plus actual damages and legal costs, creating a serious risk that the provision could be gamed and produce large taxpayer-funded payouts.

The bill makes sweeping changes to our ability to enforce a number of environmental laws. For example, a court that finds violations of the CWA’s “dredge and fill” permit system will be unable to invalidate the permit except in narrow circumstances; a court can never invalidate a permit based on a violation of the NEPA and the NHPA, no matter how severe it finds a legal violation to be. Though a deficient review can be returned to an agency, construction is allowed to continue while the agency corrects its mistakes. The result could be that by the time the agency completes its review, the project may already be largely or entirely built and the damage difficult or impossible to reverse.

Right now, if a court finds that an agency violated NEPA, it can stop the project from moving forward until the agency corrects the environmental review documents. For example, a federal judge put an oil and gas lease in Alaska’s ecologically rich Cook Inlet on hold until the responsible agency corrected its defective environmental review. That reasonable result may not have been possible had this bill been the law.

The bill also excludes activities from NEPA review, expands exemptions for others, narrows the analysis of alternatives, and potentially limits who can bring a case. Collectively, these changes substantially reduce the practical value of NEPA as a means to improve environmental outcomes. Tribes, local organizations, and affected communities may be particularly disadvantaged if they are cut out of the process or cannot stop harmful projects before they cause damage.

The bill would dramatically curtail the rights and powers of Tribes enshrined in Section 106 of the NHPA, effectively limiting Tribes’ ability to protect their lands and culturally significant places from proposed projects with a federal connection. The bill limits Tribal participation in decisions concerning federally connected projects and what Tribal interests are protected, which, under current law, includes not only artifacts but also sacred places, cultural landscapes, waterways, wildlife, and living ecosystems. Tribal Nations and Indigenous partners have made clear that these changes significantly undermine Tribal sovereignty and the federal government’s nation-to-nation responsibilities.

NHPA, specifically Section 106, has played a critical role in ensuring that permitting processes must integrate Tribal Nation feedback, helping to improve the environmental and cultural resource outcomes for projects, including the Pebble Mine and the Arches and Canyonlands National Parks, due to oil and gas drilling proposals. Proposed changes to Section 106 would place additional areas in further jeopardy—including mining proposals that would impact the Brooks Range and Gates of the Arctic National Park and Preserve, along with drilling proposals in the Chaco region, the Western Arctic, and the Arctic National Wildlife Refuge, respectively.

The bill weakens several CWA programs, which will make it easier for activities that pollute or destroy water resources to move forward without adequate safeguards. It limits the ability of states and Tribes to ensure the health of streams, lakes, wetlands, and groundwater when the federal government authorizes activities that impact them. It takes a fast-tracked permitting process meant for activities that have minimal impacts (like boat ramps) and applies it to major projects such as pipelines and highways.

The bill makes significant changes to the Clean Water Act program that gives states and Tribes the ability to demand water quality–based improvements to federal permits. For gas pipelines and transmission projects, reviewing authorities are limited to considering direct discharges, (e.g., just the effects of a concrete structure for a pipeline) rather than broader construction-related effects such as erosion, sediment, contaminated runoff, groundwater pollution, and damage to wetlands and streams, or ongoing impacts from the operation of the project.

For other projects, the bill places a substantially higher burden on states seeking to require protections. Currently, a state can identify a water quality concern, request reasonable changes, and allow a project to proceed with stronger safeguards. A state would now be required to demonstrate harm by clear and convincing evidence (versus reasonable evidence) and show that its proposed condition is the least burdensome means of addressing the water quality concern. In practice, these new hurdles to water quality conditions will be very difficult to overcome, which will likely result in fewer state conditions on permits needed to protect water quality. In addition, the bill would restrict states and Tribes from taking the actions they can today to protect habitat, groundwater (including drinking water supplies), and many small streams and critical wetlands.

How the Clean Water Act change could impact states

If the special provisions for gas pipeline projects had been the law, Pennsylvania likely would not have been able to require the Atlantic Sunrise Pipeline Project to comply with state erosion and sediment laws, and West Virginia likely would not have been able to require controls and compliance monitoring that enabled the state to enforce against the Mountain Valley Pipeline’s violations of runoff requirements.

By shifting and raising the burden of proof, this requirement would jeopardize precautionary state actions, such as a Tennessee decision this spring, when it refused to sign off on an Army Corps permit for a landfill because the project developer had failed to show that pollution from the site would not harm local waters. This kind of state engagement improves projects and does not end them.

The bill also weakens the Clean Water Act’s general permitting program (administered by the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers) for dredging and filling waters. The bill directs the Corps, when creating general permits, to look only at the harm that results from filling in waters. No other water impacts like water pollution or groundwater depletion could be considered. Additionally, right now, most general permits can only be used for impacts of one-half acre or less; this bill would quadruple this threshold, which could allow larger data centers or other major projects to qualify. It also extends the duration of general permits, reducing opportunities for public input on requirements for projects to once a decade. Finally, it requires the Corps to maintain fast-track permits for large “linear” projects that can have major environmental harms, like roadways and pipelines.

The bill weakens other Clean Water Act programs as well. It would curb the EPA’s ability to stop projects that dump dredged or fill material that “have an unacceptable adverse effect on municipal water supplies, shellfish beds and fishery areas (including spawning and breeding areas), wildlife, or recreational areas,” which the agency has invoked rarely, but done so to protect exceptional habitats threatened by highly damaging projects. It would slow the EPA’s development of scientific advice to states about the levels of pollutants that can cause harm to aquatic life or people, and it would delay updates to discharge requirements for industrial polluters and sewage plants; together, these two changes would constrain the ability to control “forever chemicals.”

Language relating to the “best available science” standard could be interpreted to restrict precautionary action when scientific information is uncertain. This is particularly concerning when an imperiled population of a species is difficult or expensive to study and waiting for definitive proof could result in irreversible loss.

The bill also allows states to assume responsibilities currently carried out by the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service. Many states lack the capacity, expertise, or in some cases, the commitment necessary to perform this responsibility effectively, and if a state is not executing its responsibility, there is not a requirement for the federal government to reassume it.

The bill would exempt many wells drilled on private lands that tap into federally owned oil and gas reserves from federal permitting, opening at least 57 million subsurface acres of federal resources to exploitation without federal permits. If passed into law, this provision strips thousands of private landowners across the West of important protections like required notice of industry’s plans to develop on their property, increases the risk that landowners get stuck with orphaned wells and their associated environmental and financial costs, and creates new risks of fraud and abuse as it relates to royalty reporting.

The bill allows mining companies to claim an unlimited number of five-acre mill sites on public lands to be used for things like tailing storage—wastewater and rock often containing heavy metals and other dangerous residues—and waste dumps. And it allows mining companies to occupy public lands for any other use relevant to a mining project, regardless of its proximity to the actual mine, meaning roads, pipelines, powerlines, and any other activity formerly requiring a federal permit and environmental review would be allowed so long as the activity is included in the mine’s operation plan.

The modeling completed to date focuses on greenhouse gas and economic impacts. Available analyses from NRDC and other groups generally project modest to significant greenhouse gas benefits, especially over the long term, but the results vary substantially depending on the provisions modeled, policy baseline, fuel and technology costs, and implementation assumptions.

NRDC’s initial results show modest power sector benefits.

The benefits of additional transmission will generally be greater in a policy environment that drives clean energy deployment. In a baseline with limited support for new clean energy resources, transmission may improve reliability and reduce costs without producing sizable emissions reductions.

The oil-and-gas effects remain uncertain. NRDC has not quantified the bill’s effects on oil-and-gas development. Because the existing baseline already assumes high levels of domestic production growth (oil and gas production have both doubled in the last 20 years), faster permitting may not produce a large increase in emissions compared with business as usual. Nevertheless, the bill could accelerate individual projects, improve their economics, and make approved infrastructure more difficult to regulate or modify later. The risk of locking in that trajectory merits consideration, even if near-term emissions changes appear modest.

Data-center growth creates a particularly important unknown. The grid provisions may indeed enable data centers to finance upgrades and connect to an expanded transmission system. But transmission takes years to plan and construct. In the interim, faster permitting and weaker environmental safeguards could encourage additional on-site or nearby gas generation, particularly in regions with access to existing pipelines or gas fields.

Greenhouse gas emissions are only one measure of the bill’s effects. The modeling does not quantify potential consequences for drinking water, local air pollution, public health, endangered species and wildlife, or other metrics. It also cannot account for the practical importance of judicial remedies in ensuring that agencies and developers comply with environmental law.

NRDC will continue to advance technical corrections, including changes needed to address drafting errors and unintended consequences. But technical corrections cannot substitute for changes to some of these structural provisions, for which we will continue to advocate.

#5827. Why Pontiac Paid The SCCA $5 For Every Trans Am It Built

Pontiac had helped launch the muscle-car era in 1963 — when it debuted the GTO package for its 1964 Pontiac Tempest LeMans coupe — and the brand followed that up with the Firebird pony car in 1967. In 1969, both saw iconic variants take the stage. The former began courting customers with a new GTO trim called The Judge, while the latter hatched the Firebird Trans Am.

Only, it wasn't called the Trans Am at first. The brand had originally tried out a variety of different ideas on the public, with "Sebring" coming out on top –- inspired, no doubt, by the country's oldest road-racing circuit, Sebring International Raceway in Sebring, Florida. Yet, when Pontiac went to register the name, it discovered Chrysler had gotten there first.

The public's next-most-popular names were "Formula" and "Trans Am," so Pontiac snapped up both. Trans Am was reserved for the most powerful member of the Firebird family, which was actually a little odd. General Motors was already running Camaros in the Sports Car Club of America's Trans Am series. Moreover, Pontiac's decision ran into a roadblock anyways. It turns out that the brand didn't have permission from the SCCA to use that moniker, at least not at first. Once the lawyers got involved, Pontiac agreed to pay the organization $5 for every Firebird Trans Am it produced.

Now, finding the exact amount forked over isn't easy, but in 1979 alone, for instance, enthusiast sites say that Pontiac made more than 117,000 Tran Ams. Royalties-wise, that works out to a non-negligible total of $585,000, which is equivalent to about $2.7 million today. Some sources say that — during some seasons — the Pontiac royalty check was all that kept the SCCA out of bankruptcy.

One of the reasons Pontiac didn't put up a fuss about the royalty deal was that it didn't think it would actually sell that many. The SCCA apparently didn't realize what was going on until 1970 or 1971, and the brand had only produced 697 Trans Ams during the model's first partial year on the market — it went on sale in April of 1969. For some context, the entire Firebird lineup, in what was considered a down year, was worth 87,709 sales during 1969.

But one of the main reasons the Trans Am was introduced was to boost demand for the Firebird family. Helping to attract enthusiast customers was a pretty comprehensive package of upgrades that would set you back $724.60 (for a total Trans Am base price that opened at about $3,600). The highlight was under the hood, where Pontiac placed a standard 400-cubic-inch V8 with a Ram Air III intake system good for 330 bhp. As an alternative, buyers could opt for a more powerful setup with 345 bhp. It's backed by the same displacement, plus high-lift cams and upgraded valves/pistons. Additionally, there were standard dynamic details such as front/rear spoilers, functional hood scoops, a ride-and-handling package, high-effort variable-ratio power steering, high-effort power front disc brakes, and dual exhaust. Of course, when it comes to exhaust outlets, two isn't always better than one.

All '69 Trans Ams were then wrapped in a Cameo White exterior accented by Tyrol Blue racing stripes. One thing that did set some apart, however, was the body style. The majority of the first-year cars – 689 -– were hardtops, but 8 were convertibles.

Currently presented by Pirelli — and originally known as the Trans American Sedan Championship — the series was just about to wrap up its 60th-anniversary season at the Circuit of the Americas when this article was written. The very first race was held in 1966, and in an interesting coincidence, it was at Sebring.

The first years of the series might have been its golden era, too. That's when it was a high-performance playground for pony cars such as the Camaro Z/28, Mustang Boss 302, Dodge Challenger T/A, and AMC Javelin. But what's ironic is that the 1969 Pontiac Firebird Trans Am, the one that first borrowed the Trans Am name from the SCCA, never raced in the series because its engine was too big for the rulebook. That said, the occasional Pontiac Trans Am did show up in the series' record books. The highlight? Sports-car master Elliot Forbes-Robinson drove his Trans Am racecar to five victories and the series championship in 1982.

There were some big names on hand as well. That first Trans Am race at Sebring was won by Jochen Rindt, who would go on to claim the 1970 Formula 1 driver's championship. The likes of A.J. Foyt, Jacky Ickx, Richard Petty, and Mark Donohue also competed in the series' early seasons. Meanwhile, after a few decades with a more international focus – Jaguar, for one, scored multiple driver's and manufacturer's championships in the early 2000s — Trans Am racing has returned to American muscle in recent years, and that's even though some folks don't think muscle cars have to be American. The 2026 field is packed with Chevrolet Camaros and Ford Mustangs.

#5825. AI Comes For Drag Racers' Jobs As GM Patents Automated Launch Control

AI is coming for all of us. Not necessarily in an apocalyptic world like "The Terminator" or "The Matrix," but by stealing jobs from truck drivers, astronauts, and even Jalopnik writers (despite what I read in the comments, I assure you we're all human beings — at least, for now). Not even drag racers are safe, thanks to a launch control system GM patented that not only automates the launch process, but even reads the countdown Christmas tree to time a perfect launch.

Patents can be wordy and cumbersome to read, but Road & Track sums this one up nicely. Some cars already have launch control systems, which can get you off the line as quickly as possible with the perfect balance of power and traction. Pair those systems with the cameras being used in cars today and the rest is a simple matter of programming.

The potential future tech uses the car's cameras to recognize the Christmas tree lights at a drag strip, and a prompt instructs the driver to activate launch control. This part works like normal, with the driver pressing the gas and brake pedals simultaneously. Once launch control is engaged, the driver removes their feet from the pedals, and the car takes over. It doesn't just use its onboard cameras to watch the lights and go on green, it initiates the launch process before the light is green, ensuring the car begins to move precisely when it's supposed to without red-lighting or launching too early. This is exactly the way I learned to do it, but a computer is going to be far more precise than my feet. I'm only human.

Automatic drag strip launch control is a fine technological achievement. It also completely misses the point of what racing is all about: human drivers testing their skill against one another. Drag racing doesn't have the braking or handling challenges of a road course or rally stage, but it still requires skill to reduce your reaction time and execute even a near-perfect launch. If you take that out of the equation by automating the entire process, what's left? Not steering into the wall? In a production car, that takes even less skill than driving down the highway. (Top Fuel dragsters and Funny Cars are a completely different story. Mad respect to them.)

Does anyone really want autonomous racing? I sure don't. In theory, a machine can always put down the perfect lap, time after time. The only time it gets exciting is when the programming goes wrong, and it steers straight into a wall. People already complain that Formula 1 is boring. It takes extraordinary driver talent to race at those speeds, but the cars are so good, so reliable, and so evenly matched that there's little difference between them. Take the driver out of the car, and it's nothing but a competition of technology. If I want to see that, I'd rather watch BattleBots. It's much more fun, and you get to watch them completely destroy each other.

I have never driven a perfect lap, and I never will. Perfection itself doesn't matter. It's the pursuit of perfection that matters. Striving to do better than we ever have before is rewarding for its own sake. It's also part of what makes us human. So I'll leave GM's drag strip launch control turned off and drop the clutch myself. I don't care that I'll run a slower time than the fully automated machine. As a certain James Bond villain once said, "There's no point in living if you can't feel alive."
