#5824. Retatrutide Is One Click Away. That Doesn't Make it Safe.

— Promising data on the real drug tell us little about what's in a gray-market vial

A few clicks, a credit card, and a package arrives at your door. The same technology that has expanded access to information and consumer goods has also made it easier than ever for unregulated products to reach consumers while masquerading as legitimate medicine.

As an endocrinologist who treats obesity and diabetes, I have watched new therapies transform care for a complex chronic disease. I also regularly have patients asking about products they found online, on social media, at a medical spa, or through friends and family. Their curiosity and desire for affordable treatment options make sense. But their safety depends on knowing what a product actually is, and whether it has been tested to the standards we expect of any medicine.

Those standards exist for good reason. Before a complex medication reaches patients, it goes through years of laboratory research and progressively larger clinical trials that establish whether it works, for which patients, at what dose, and with what risks. It is then produced by an approved manufacturer under strict quality controls, in facilities subject to inspection, and monitored for safety after it reaches the market. This system allows a physician to safely prescribe a drug for a specific condition, and a patient to trust what is in their syringe.

Semaglutide (Ozempic, Wegovy) and tirzepatide (Mounjaro, Zepbound) went through that process and were approved by FDA. But products sold online or at medical spas using the same ingredient names, semaglutide and tirzepatide, do not automatically carry the same safeguards.

Their success has fueled excitement about what comes next.

Retatrutide, often marketed online as "Reta" or "GLP-3," is the latest example. (Side note: the nickname is a misnomer. The molecule acts on three hormone receptors -- GLP-1, GIP, and glucagon -- making it more accurately a "triple-G" agonist.) Results from phase 3 clinical trials in obesity and type 2 diabetes were recently presented at the European Association for the Study of Diabetes meeting in Milan, with simultaneous publication in the New England Journal of Medicine and The Lancet. The results are impressive, but retatrutide remains investigational and is not approved for any use.

Just as important, the retatrutide studied in those trials is not what is being sold online. Clinical trial participants receive drugs made to exacting specifications, at carefully defined doses and escalation schedules, under close medical monitoring. A gray-market vial labeled "retatrutide" may or may not contain the actual molecule. It may contain more or less than the label claims, or impurities and contaminants no one has tested for. And because there is no established dose for a product of unknown content, buyers are left to mix and inject based on guesswork from online forums. Promising data on the real drug tell us little about what is in that gray-market vial.

The FDA's position is explicit: federal law does not permit retatrutide to be compounded or sold. The agency notes that retatrutide is not an ingredient in any FDA-approved drug and has not been shown to be safe and effective for any condition. Calling a product "compounded retatrutide" does not make it an approved or lawful treatment, and a "for research use only" label does not make it safe. The FDA urges consumers not to buy these products, warning that their quality is unknown and they may harm patients' health.

The agency has also taken enforcement action. In a March 2026 warning letter to Gram Peptides, FDA identified products marketed as retatrutide as unapproved new drugs and said introducing them into interstate commerce violated federal law. It warned that injectables can cause serious harm because they bypass the body's key defenses against toxins and microorganisms. No professional-looking website or glowing testimonial can confirm a product's identity, strength, purity, or sterility.

We, as clinicians, must help patients navigate this landscape without judgment. We need to create a space where patients feel comfortable bringing advertisements and questions into the exam room, where we can review the evidence together and address access issues.

My advice to my patients is clear: do not buy or use retatrutide until it is FDA approved and available from the legitimate manufacturer. In the meantime, I encourage them to ask me or another provider which FDA-approved treatments may fit their needs and how to obtain them through a licensed pharmacy. If investigational treatments interest them, I encourage them to ask about legitimate clinical trials.

Technology can support informed healthcare decisions, but it cannot replace medical guidance. The next step toward better health should begin with a patient-doctor conversation -- not an online checkout.

#5823. GM Steps On Tesla’s EV Toes With EV1 Celebration

In a move that shocked and surprised nobody, last week Tesla CEO Elon Musk pulled the plug on his much-hyped Cybertruck. Production will end sometime next year. It may be small consolation, but at least the Cybertruck sold more units than another notorious flop in modern automotive history, General Motors’s ill-fated EV1 sedan. Was EV1 really a flop, though? In sales, yes, but GM wants everyone to know that the EV1 beat Tesla to the electrification punch in key technology milestones.

GM actually sold few, if any, EV1 units, preferring to lease the car with a focus on drivers in California. Production began in 1996 but that didn’t last long. In 2003 GM pulled the plug, recalled the vehicles, and sent them to the crusher, having produced barely more than 1,000 units overall.

Only a scant few escaped the junkyard. One of them was rescued by US filmmaker Alex Gibney, leading to his advisory role in the searing 2006 EV1 documentary “Who Killed the Electric Car?” (btw, Gibney ‘s newly released “Musk” documentary is available on streaming now).

This year marks the 30th anniversary of EV1 production, and GM is using the occasion to celebrate. Rather than shoveling all memory of the EV1 debacle into the memory hole, GM has embarked on sort of under-the-radar public relations campaign, seeking to position the car as a necessary, albeit short lived, step along the vehicle electrification journey.

In not so many words, GM also draws attention to the fact that its work on EV1 predates the launch of Tesla Motors, which came on the scene in 2003. The automaker’s Senior Writer and Editor at GM News, Chris Perkins, ran down the particulars in March, noting that EV1 was the first EV to deploy heat pumps for climate control, energy efficiency, and battery temperature management.

Perkins also takes note of the car’s regenerative braking system. “Engineers developed a system for the car that translated a driver’s brake-pedal input into an electronic signal that blended regenerative and friction braking,” Perkins wrote.

“It’s a precursor to the braking systems used in GM’s modern EVs, which also add One-Pedal Driving1 and paddle-actuated Regen-On-Demand2 capability,” he added.

EV1 also eschewed mechanical actuators in favor of fully electronic (aka by-wire) controls for the accelerator pedal, brake pedal, parking brake, and gear selector, with the power steering featuring electro-hydraulic control.

Additionally, Perkins elaborated on the regenerative braking angle in a follow-up article in August, by way of demonstrating a through line between the 1990’s technology and the automaker’s current EV lineup.

“Conceptually, the EV1’s braking system operates exactly like the braking systems in GM’s modern EVs,” Perkins wrote. “Press the brake pedal, and the car’s computers decide how much friction and regenerative braking to actuate. Should the electronic system fail, it’s connected to a mechanical backup, just as in the EV1.”

As part of the PR campaign, GM is also putting its 1994 concept sedan on display, the 1994 Impact (pictured above). “As one of the first modern, purpose-built electric vehicles from a major automaker, the Impact was a critical learning tool that shaped the final production version of the EV1,” GM emphasizes.

If you blink, you’ll miss it. The Impact is on display at the GM-sponsored Test Track at EPCOT, the Disney theme park in Bay Lake, Florida, until mid-December.

As for why all this fuss, why now, that’s a good question. Over the past several years, GM has put a jolly spin on its inability to catch up to Tesla in sales, let alone surpass it. As recently as last year, GM vigorously touted itself as #2 in EV sales in the US, second only to Tesla as a badge of honor.

Still, by August of 2025 the competition was beginning to take on a different tone, with GM pitching low-cost LFP (lithium-iron-phosphate) batteries as a near-term pathway to meeting, then beating Tesla.

The 2026 EV1 celebration elaborates upon the technology angle, underscoring GM’s claim on the pre-Tesla, 1990’s roots of innovation in the vehicle electrification field.

The new emphasis on technology also comes at a pivotal moment for EV sales in the US. The US market nosedived last fall after US President Trump and his Republican allies in Congress prematurely eliminated federal tax credits for EVs. However, activity continued to stir in some quarters, and Trump himself made the case for EVs more attractive when he decided to bomb Iran in February.

Nine months later, the price of gas remains stubbornly high, sparking renewed hopes that EV sales will rebound more quickly than first anticipated. In addition, a fresh round of innovation is on the horizon, with GM banking on its forthcoming LMR (lithium manganese-rich) battery formula to push costs down without sacrificing performance.

While Tesla is not the only competition in town, beating the startup at its own game would be a feather in GM’s cap, and Elon Musk made the effort a little easier when he canceled the Cybertruck, leaving Tesla without a foothold in the hot market for pickup trucks in the US. The automaker still has sedans, SUVs, the new Semi Class 8 truck, and the “flying” Roadster in its pocket, but the demise of the Cybertruck has left the pickup field wide open.

Meanwhile, Ford is on track to produce its new Fathom electric pickup next year starting at under $30,000, far less than the Cybertruck’s most recent starting price of $77,000 plus change. The Jeff Bezos-backed startup Slate Auto is also aiming at the affordability market with a stripped-down electric pickup starting at a base price of $26,000 and change, before accounting for add-ons.

On its part, GM is aiming for the middle ground with the 2027 Silverado electric pickup, starting at around $56,000 and reaching close to Cybertruck range at around $72,000.

Meanwhile, Rivian is also aiming upscale at close to $80,000 and up for its RIT pickup. The startup is on the move, having somehow managed to squeeze a loan guarantee of up to $4.5 billion out of the Trump administration. The funds are earmarked to expand Rivian’s production capacity with a new factory in Georgia.

Readers, what do you think? Does GM — or any other automaker — have a snowball’s chance in hell to catch up to Tesla in the US market? Drop a note in the discussion thread…

Photo: General Motors introduced the Impact concept EV in 1994, laying the groundwork for the automaker’s short-lived EV1 electric car (Impact concept; cropped, courtesy of GM).

#5822. So You've Hit A Deer With Your Car. Now What?

Fall is a magical time of year: The air is alive with the scent of pumpkin spice, the decorative gourds are presented, and, of course, the dang deer won't stay off the roads. Typical fall, right? That last one ain't no joke — just about everyone who has driven in a place with a significant deer population can tell you a tale or two about a run-in with deer. If you're in France, you really need to look out for the drunk deer.

Deer are a hazard drivers have to contend with. Sure, we could put some murder kitties in the forests, because more big cats in forests can reduce car crashes by roughly 75%. Or, we could install crossings to give creatures a safe path over big roads, like they did in California with the world's largest wildlife crossing. But short of that, accidents with deer will happen. State Farm reports that there were more than 1.6 million animal-related collisions between July 2025 and July 2026. It is a real concern.

But don't fret. If the unfortunate accident does happen, the first thing you should do is to ensure your own safety. Move off the road, and turn on your hazard lights so you're not at risk from any other vehicles. Check your vehicle only when it's safe to do so. There's no need to compound the accident by putting yourself in greater danger.

Hopefully, you are in a safer situation now, so be sure to check any passengers and yourself for injuries. Call 911 immediately if anyone is injured. At this point, you may be tempted to check on the deer. If you can see it and it's a road hazard, for safety's sake, report it. You don't want another driver to hit it. Do not attempt to approach or move it! An injured animal is a dangerous animal. If it's not visible, don't try to find it.

At this point, it's not a bad idea to take pictures of the accident in case your insurance asks for it. Your insurance may also ask for an accident report, so it's a good idea to get one. Speaking of insurance, hitting a deer is usually covered under comprehensive coverage if you have it. Swerving to miss a deer and hitting something else is typically covered by collision coverage, but don't do that.

If your vehicle is not drivable, call a tow truck. If you think your car is still drivable, you may be tempted to leave. If there is property damage or if the deer is still a hazard to others, report it. Otherwise, depending on state law, you may be okay to leave. Before you drive off, do a basic check of your vehicle to ensure that it's actually roadworthy. Take a look underneath your vehicle to see if it is leaking any fluids. If it is, do not drive it — you can cause more damage to your engine. Check that the hood is latched securely and will not come loose. Verify the headlights are still working, especially when it's dark out. Simple stuff, but it could save you trouble down the road.

There is no sure-fire way to avoid hitting a deer, but you can reduce your risk by being cautious when you're in an area with an active deer population. Slow down to a speed that will allow you a better chance of stopping before they become hood ornaments. Be especially cautious at dawn and dusk, as deer are more prone to roam at those times of day. Use extra caution when traveling near wildlife crossing signs. No, the deer aren't reading those signs and deciding to cross there – obviously, those signs declare that you are in an area known to have heavy activity. Also, remember that deer tend to travel in groups, so if you see one, others are likely nearby.

Lastly, if hitting that deer is unavoidable, your natural instinct will be to swerve to avoid the animal.  Fight the urge to do this. Swerving to miss the deer is often more dangerous, as it can cause your car to roll or result in other unwanted behavior. Quite often, the resulting crash is worse than just hitting the deer. Brake in a straight line, and brace for impact.

#5820. Cold Seawater Is Supplying District Heat in Esbjerg, Denmark

Esbjerg, Denmark, is using large electric heat pumps to extract heat from the North Sea and supply its district-heating network. During a two-hour winter test, seawater entered the system at 3.3°C and left at 1.2°C. The two heat pumps consumed 19.9 MW of electricity and supplied 55.2 MW of heat at a district-heating water temperature of 90°C. The difference, 35.3 MW, came from the seawater. The project team’s May 2025 operating report recorded a coefficient of performance, or COP, of 2.8. The figures describe that test, not annual average performance.

A heat pump transfers thermal energy from a colder source to a warmer destination. Its refrigerant absorbs heat at a temperature below that of the seawater, and an electrically driven compressor raises the temperature so the heat can enter the district network. Esbjerg uses carbon dioxide as its refrigerant in a high-pressure cycle. For each unit of electricity used by the compressors during the test, the plant delivered 2.8 units of heat. Resistance heating would have required 2.8 times as much electricity for the same heat output under those conditions.

The installation has a nominal heating capacity of 70 MW and began delivering heat in late 2024, as part of Esbjerg’s replacement of its retired coal-fired combined heat and power plant. The operating report describes controls for variable conditions and protection against freezing as seawater temperatures fall. The recorded COP of 2.8 was lower than the more favourable performance figures used in the original project expectations, and full guarantee testing had not been completed when the results were published. The city’s heating supply also includes a wood-chip boiler and waste-incineration heat. Emissions reductions reported for the wider replacement programme cannot be attributed in full to the seawater heat pumps.

Electricity price and heating-network temperature have a direct effect on the cost. At an illustrative electricity price of €100/MWh, compressor power at COP 2.8 costs about €36 per MWh of useful heat. That excludes seawater pumping, equipment maintenance, capital recovery, financing and heat distribution. A network able to operate at lower water temperatures generally asks the compressor to make a smaller temperature increase, which can improve COP. Older networks supplying 90°C heat face a harder operating requirement than newer, lower-temperature networks.

Esbjerg builds on decades of seawater heating experience. Monaco began using seawater heat pumps in 1963, and Stockholm has used large seawater-sourced district-heating equipment since the 1980s. Creative Energy’s Horseshoe Bay development in West Vancouver takes a different approach. Submerged heat exchangers transfer heat through a closed loop, with no seawater intake or discharge to the marina. Denmark’s Aalborg project is developing 177 MW of seawater heat-pump capacity. These installations serve different loads and use different marine arrangements, so their costs cannot be assumed to match Esbjerg’s.

Marine heat systems require more than suitable water temperatures. Engineers must address corrosion, biological fouling, intake and discharge effects, pumping requirements, maintenance access and freezing protection. The environmental assessment has to consider the local marine ecosystem and the discharge of colder water. The distribution network can be the larger financial obstacle in areas without existing pipes or concentrated heat demand. Wastewater, industrial waste heat, ground-source systems or individual air-source heat pumps may provide lower-cost heat at some sites.

Hot-water storage can add value by allowing a utility to make some heat when electricity is inexpensive and deliver it later. The available flexibility depends on storage capacity, network temperatures and heat demand. Esbjerg’s test provides direct evidence that cold seawater can support high-temperature district heating. Coastal utilities can use that evidence when comparing local heat sources, network investments and the costs of replacing combustion-based heating.

My TFIE Strategy Briefing assessment examines Esbjerg’s operating results, experience in Stockholm and Monaco, the Horseshoe Bay system near Vancouver, and the cost and environmental factors that determine where seawater heating is suitable.

#5819. Here's How Much AAA Says It Costs To Own A Car In 2026

When we consider whether we can afford a car, so much of the focus tends to be on the sticker price that we often forget that the costs don't stop once we've made our purchase. Small, everyday expenses that come alongside, like fuel, servicing, finance interest, depreciation, insurance, and tax, aren't always obvious, but the true cost of car ownership adds up over time.

With that in mind, the car valuation experts at AAA performed a study to investigate car ownership costs in 2026. It turns out that drivers are facing ongoing price increases, with the AAA 2026 Your Driving Costs study revealing that the annual cost of owning and running a new car has soared to $12,863, or $1,071.92 per month this year. That's up from an average of $11,577 or $964.78 per month in 2025.

At that rate, ownership costs can add 32.67% on top of the $39,376 sales-weighted average MSRP of new vehicles. The larger bills have been linked to surging fuel prices, faster depreciation, and higher finance interest rates. Still, your specific costs can vary greatly, depending on your car's fuel type.

Owning any car at all is getting more expensive, but the AAA study revealed something more fundamental: Electric cars cost more to own than their traditional fuel-powered and hybrid counterparts. That's largely because depreciation on EVs is worse than gas or hybrid cars. On top of that, those who drive electric cars face higher fees and finance costs. Where EVs tend to do better is in fuel expenses, as they typically cost 66% to 70% less to run than gasoline cars.

Looking at a set of average consumption figures, AAA found that regular-grade gasoline costs $4.152 per gallon on average, while electric cars charged at home averaged as little as 18 cents per kilowatt hour. EVs have seen smaller electricity rate increases, too. The AAA data shows electricity prices have jumped 7.8% since 2025, while gas costs have increased a shocking 31.8%.

Even so, owning and running EVs costs more than gas-powered models, due to higher fees, finance costs, and depreciation, with certain EVs said to depreciate about twice as fast as their gas-powered counterparts. That contributed to pushing EV ownership costs above gas-powered models across the medium sedan, compact SUV, and pickup truck segments.

Nowhere is that gap more pronounced than in the medium sedan segment, where gas-powered medium sedans cost $3,080 less to own (at $10,582 per year) than comparable EV medium sedans ($13,662). Hybrids are even cheaper (at $10,204) and cost the least to own in every category, including the medium SUV class, where EVs win back some ground against gas-powered models, costing $14,332 versus $14,431 for gasoline SUVs.

As a car owner, every mile you drive costs money, but it is entirely possible to keep costs down. One way to do this is to shop around for cheaper insurance. Compare quotes from providers, or even consider buying a car from one of the cheapest brands to insure.

If you are team gas-powered cars, getting a model with great fuel efficiency is just as important. It should be easy enough, seeing as gasoline cars are now much more efficient than they used to be, with some of the most fuel-efficient models released over the years rated to return as high as 58 mpg.

You'll also want to consider depreciation. It is one of the single largest ownership costs and can add a weighted average of $4,422 per year to the cost of running some popular models, according to the AAA study. Toyota, Subaru, and Honda are some of the best brands for value retention, but if you're after something more premium, there's always Lexus. It's the luxury car brand with the best resale value, according to CarEdge.

However, maintenance and spare parts are usually more expensive for luxury marques than mainstream brands like Toyota or Honda. Speaking of which, staying on top maintenance is yet another important part of vehicle ownership that can help keep costs low. Not only does it help prevent larger bills down the road, keeping up with car maintenance also provides a strong service history that supports resale value when it comes time to sell.

#5818. Lp(a)-Lowering Pelacarsen Shows Huge Disconnect With Cardiovascular Outcomes

— After disappointing Lp(a) HORIZON trial, eyes turn to next-gen siRNA therapies

Lowering lipoprotein(a), or Lp(a), did not translate into better cardiovascular outcomes in a secondary prevention population, at least not with pelacarsen in the Lp(a) HORIZON trial.

Among people with elevated lipoprotein(a) and pre-existing cardiovascular disease (CVD), pelacarsen was no help for reducing the primary endpoint of cardiovascular death, nonfatal stroke, nonfatal myocardial infarction (MI), or urgent coronary revascularization over nearly 5 years (HR 1.02 compared with placebo, 95% CI 0.90-1.15), reported Steven Nissen, MD, of the Cleveland Clinic, at the American Heart Association (AHA) annual meeting in Chicago.

No matter how the investigators sliced and diced the data, it was the same story: analysis of people with especially high lipoprotein(a), 90 mg/dL or higher, also yielded no benefit (HR 1.00, 95% CI 0.87-1.15); pelacarsen similarly showed no efficacy regarding a modified cardiovascular endpoint not counting revascularizations, another composite endpoint including coronary heart disease rather than cardiovascular deaths, and the individual outcomes of MI, stroke, urgent revascularization, and cardiovascular death.

Beyond these "completely neutral" results, "tolerability issues were certainly very prominent" with pelacarsen, Nissen added during an AHA press conference, citing rates of adverse events leading to drug discontinuation of 20.6% with pelacarsen versus 7.5% with placebo.

Nissen stressed that it may be the end of the road for pelacarsen, but not the lipoprotein(a) hypothesis.

"The Lp(a) HORIZON trial is not the end of the story. Ongoing trials are studying different populations, like primary prevention, aortic stenosis, and different therapies, and siRNA, several siRNAs. A single trial does not provide definitive evidence of a lack of benefit of lowering lipoprotein(a) as a strategy to reduce cardiovascular risk," he said.

Lipoprotein(a) is a genetically determined risk factor for atherosclerotic CVD and aortic stenosis. It is a highly atherogenic particle considered unmodifiable with diet or physical activity, unlike LDL cholesterol. Estimates suggest one in five people worldwide have high lipoprotein(a).

Pelacarsen was an antisense oligonucleotide made to degrade the hepatic mRNA coding for apolipoprotein(a), an intermediate to the production of lipoprotein(a).

In Lp(a) HORIZON, pelacarsen did drastically reduce lipoprotein(a) and LDL cholesterol by an estimated 77.7% and 13.3%, respectively, relative to placebo. This was on top of existing secondary prevention therapies that had gotten baseline LDL cholesterol to a median 64.6 mg/dL and systolic blood pressure to 125 mmHg on average.

"Was there no room left for improvement? To the credit of the investigators, what was done was actually optimization of what we know to do already: optimize the LDL, optimize the blood pressure. If we do that, was there just no room left in these patients to further reduce the risk?" posed panelist Donald Lloyd-Jones, MD, ScM, of Boston University.

"Like Dr. Nissen, I personally would not recommend that we abandon considering Lp(a) as a potential causal risk factor or as a therapeutic target until we have a lot more data available in different patient populations, certainly in younger individuals and primary prevention populations, over longer periods of time and with ... different chemical strategies to try to inhibit this molecule," said Lloyd-Jones, a past president of the AHA.

Nissen noted that the siRNA therapies in development are potentially more tolerable and more effective while requiring less frequent administration. Already advancing to large-scale cardiovascular outcome trials, for example, are lepodisiran and olpasiran, with others further back in the pipeline.

There's also evidence that the now-familiar PCSK9 monoclonal antibodies reduce Lp(a) along with LDL cholesterol, which may partly explain some of their benefit in CVD risk reduction, according to Lloyd-Jones.

"We don't fully understand the biology here, and I think we need to continue to take a deeper dive into that biology so that we fully understand what it is about Lp(a) that serves as a marker of risk and potentially as a better target for our future therapies," he said.

"I really think you cannot close the door with a single negative trial," Nissen emphasized. "It's going to be my mission to try to convince the people that pay the bills, which is industry sponsors, not to pull the plug on trials because we really need to understand more."

Lp(a) HORIZON trial was a phase III cardiovascular outcomes trial conducted in nearly 800 sites in 42 countries. Eligible participants had a cardiovascular event 3 months to 10 years prior to enrollment and lipoprotein(a) levels 70 mg/dL or greater. They underwent a risk factor optimization period to ensure use of secondary prevention therapies.

Nissen's group had 8,350 individuals randomized 1:1 to pelacarsen 80 mg or placebo self-administered once monthly subcutaneously.

Mean age was just under 60, with about 27% of participants being women and 78% white. Median lipoprotein(a) was 236 nmol/L and hsCRP 0.8 mg/L. Nearly 80% of the cohort were on high-intensity statins.

Follow-up reached a median 57 months in the trial.

Nissen reported that his group sought to conduct additional exploratory analyses on account of the "unexpected" results of Lp(a) HORIZON.

In this extension report, there was still no argument to be made for pelacarsen's efficacy even after accounting for treatment adherence, first and repeated adverse events, and magnitude of 3-month lipoprotein(a) reductions, among other analyses.

Lp(a) HORIZON trial was simultaneously published in the New England Journal of Medicine and its extension report separately released in NEJM Evidence.

#5817. The Velotric GoMad Electric Utility eBike — CleanTechnica Tested

Velotric has emerged as one of the largest ebike brands in the US, offering a wide range of models for buyers to choose from. Having a wide range of models with differing capabilities is increasingly a key factor for buyers when deciding which ebike to buy, as it allows them to upgrade or swap out for a different model to accommodate different stages of life.

They reached out to CleanTechnica about a review and we were excited to play with the Velotric GoMad Electric Utility bike, because it is just so darn flexible in what it can do. You can throw a set of bags on the back rack or a passenger kit to bring a friend with you. You can put a basket on the back and deliver pizzas, or you can just throw a backpack on and ride around town solo. It truly looked like the jack of all trades, so we pulled the trigger, and after a few days, it showed up.

Disclaimer: Velotric provided the GoMad to the author for the purposes of this review.

Assembling the Velotric GoMad is similar to the process for most e-bikes. It can be done with a basic set of tools that are included with the bike, and takes between 30 minutes and an hour depending on how much of a hurry you’re in.

After that, it’s a simple matter of attaching the pedals, mounting the handlebars to the stem, installing the front wheel and tire, connecting a few of the electrical connectors between the handlebars and the bike itself, airing up the tires, and you’re on your way. Ours took a few minutes longer than normal to bolt on the optional Passenger Kit

Taking in the Velotric GoMad, it is an attractive bike with great proportions. The battery is integrated into the main downtube on the frame, which makes it look slightly bloated, but in a way that fits into the overall proportions of the bike. The oversized tires help with this, making it look like it can go absolutely anywhere.

The rear hub motor kicks out plenty of power, and with a range of pedal assist modes. You can choose just how much power you need for the ride you want. You can choose from the motor being completely off, Eco, Tour, Trail, Sport, and even the full-out Boost mode that can give you exactly the support you need.

It’s perfect for when you’re carrying a load, powering up a hill, or just feeling tired. The motor is always ready to step in to provide assistance. At the upper end of its power cycle, the motor controller is more sensitive to the pedaling cadence, resulting in the motor pulsing on and off, providing for a bit of a bumpy sensation when pedaling. It’s only something you’d notice if you’re really paying attention, but it’s there.

The GoMad is designed with an integrated rear rack and a hidden storage pocket. The rack can also be converted into a seat for a second passenger with Velotric’s passenger kit. The passenger kit itself is amazing if that’s what you’re looking for, and this is further accentuated by the bike’s compact footprint. The tradeoff is that the main seat has a flat rear, which does make it slightly less comfortable than more fully built-out options.

The passenger kit comes with a set of pegs down below for the passengers’ feet to rest on, a rear grab rail for the rack, and a front handle for the passenger to hang onto as you’re boosting around town. Given the compact footprint of the bike, it feels like it was designed to be used as more of a teenager-plus-one setup, but if you want to put it to work as a husband-and-wife date night setup, its 500 pound weight capacity is more than up to the task.

I rode around on it with my wife on the back and it was very comfortable and stable for both of us. The foot pegs and the solid support bars that come with the passenger kit make it feel much safer and more comfortable for the passenger. I took a few pics of us on the bike, but, hilariously, none of them had the bike in frame and she wasn’t a fan of my one handed stunts. Of course, that’s for you to decide what you want to do with your life and how you want to set up your bike and put it to use.

The Velotric Nomad is an extremely capable bike at a mid-level price point for bikes of this quality and capability. It’s currently listed as $1,899 with a special Black Friday offer that includes a free young passenger kit.

The fact that its 750W continuous power output motor has a peak of 1,300W means it’s got plenty of pep to take even the largest and least-in-shape riders wherever they want to go. The specs across the board and the integration of the torque and cadence sensor make it feel like a very natural ride that will surprise you with just how intuitively the power is coming from the motor.

I especially love the colorways this bike comes in. They have a nice modern-looking sage that feels classy and refined, a dark amber that’s somewhere between a bright orange and bright red that looks like a pop of lipstick that really sets the whole frame off, and finally an obsidian, which is what our review bike came in.

The obsidian has a base color that looks almost black, but then when you put it in the sunlight, it has a rainbow pop of color that peeks out every once in a while. It’s not so much that it feels like it’s covered in glitter, but it’s just enough to make it feel fun.

For more information about the Velotric Nomad e-bike, head over to their official website, where you can learn all about it or purchase one for yourself.

#5816. 5 Classic Pony Cars And Their Modern Equivalents

Imagining a collage of objects of American culture, the mind conjures up images of things like sports stadiums, a drive-thru menu, the Wall Street Bull, the Hollywood sign, blue jeans, apple pie, and likely, some kind of car. Cars, our car dependency, and the American love for V8 engines are integral to our culture, and there are no cars to demonstrate this better than the pony car family. While very similar, there are some differences between a muscle car and a pony car.

To put it simply, the muscle car and the pony car are two sides of the same coin. The muscle car was bigger and purely focused on looking cool and going fast, with not much thought to anything else. The pony car took all that was fun about the muscle car, including the good looks and exciting performance, and made it all a bit easier to live with, often by being smaller than its muscle car counterparts. The Mustang started the pony car trend, but it wasn't the only one to do it. Since those early days in the 1960s, we've seen different takes from different manufacturers, including models like the Chevrolet Camaro, the Dodge Challenger, and even some from the hands of Carroll Shelby. Many of these models have stuck around to the modern day. The spirit of the pony car is old, but it is far from gone.

The Chevrolet Camaro and the Ford Mustang have been in a constant battle for the pony car crown since the 1960s. As they chug on and on, new trims and upgrades grace each car, and in 1969, we saw a Camaro born of the pure rebellious nature a pony car should represent. The legend of the ZL1 starts with a man called Fred Gibb. Gibb was a Chevrolet dealer who was particularly sick of the brand's internal practices. The Corvette was the monarch of the Chevrolet lineup, and Chevy wanted to keep it that way. It adamantly ensured that no performance car other than the Corvette could be fitted with an engine with over 400 cubic inches of displacement. Gibb was sick of this favoritism, and he knew the Camaro could be so much more. So, he did something about it.

Gibb contacted Chevy's Central Office Production Order, a division charged with custom orders for mundane civil and municipal services, building things like taxi cabs or police cars. Ordering from COPO was something like a deli sandwich counter for cars with no questions asked. You could mix and match parts, and that's exactly what Gibb wanted. He ordered 50 Camaros stripped down for light weight and fitted with 430-horsepower, 427-cubic-inch V8s sourced from Chevy's Can-Am race cars. Chevrolet quickly wised up to Gibb's loophole and shut down production, but the original ZL1 remains the stuff of pony car legend.

The ZL1 is Chevy's story of childhood rebellion, and even though Chevy didn't see the greatness of a high-powered stripped-down Camaro originally, it eventually came around to the idea. To see just how far the company has come from its Corvette-rules-all philosophy, we can look at the most recent, and final, example of the ZL1 from 2024.

What would have been blasphemy in 1969 was now standard procedure, as the 2024 ZL1 was powered by a pushrod V8 pulled straight from the C7 generation Corvette making 650 horsepower thanks to some help from a supercharger. Keeping classic pony car character, the ZL1 sends all that power strictly to the rear wheels, and it can be distributed via either a 10-speed automatic or a six speed manual transmission. If you really want to turn things up, you can opt for the 1LE package, which throws in some extra upgrades, and you don't have to go through COPO to do it. The 1LE adds some stickier tires, carbon fiber everywhere, adjustable suspension, and a rear seat delete. It's Chevrolet's love letter to a car it originally didn't want to exist.

So, the Camaro has its defiant ZL1 package, but what does the Mustang have to match it? The answer is the Shelby GT500, whose original iteration came before the ZL1 in 1967. If you know a thing or two about Ford performance cars, you'll recognize the name Shelby. Before Carroll Shelby ever had a Mustang with his name on it, he was busy stuffing his nimble European-esque Cobras with massive Ford engines that had no business being there and helping Ford beat Ferrari at Le Mans. After that former achievement, in 1967, Shelby convinced Ford to put the Le Mans-based and Le Mans-winning 428 V8 into the Mustang. And so, the GT500 was born.

Prior to the GT500, Ford had already made the GT350, which was raucously fast but a bit unpolished. The GT500 took the GT350 recipe, smoothed out the edges, and eliminated the almost homemade character. By no means did this mean that the GT500 was a tame car, though. Covered in aggressive aerodynamic body panels of fiberglass for lighter weight, the GT500's V8 made 355 horsepower, and could cover the quarter mile in 15 seconds, ripping past the line at 95 mph. It was a race-bred Mustang for the road, a hot-rodder's garage build in a suit and a Stetson, and it was one of the wickedly cool cars that made Carroll Shelby a legend.

Fast forward to 53 years later, the Shelby GT500 nameplate lived on. Although the newest S650 generation of Mustang drops the GT500 trim in favor of the Dark Horse SC, the S550 received the Shelby treatment for the 2020 model. As with the original, the 2020 GT500 is very clearly not your average Mustang. If the massive hood bulge, aggressive wing, and imposing front fascia aren't enough to convince you this car means business, the exhaust note certainly should. Thanks to its cross-plane crankshaft, the GT500 produces an all-American muscle car growl with a throaty bass.

Under the hood is a 5.2-liter V8, christened "Predator" by Ford, making a whopping 760 horsepower, thanks, in part, to the Eaton-supplied supercharger, which makes 12 psi of boost. The GT500 has brains to match the brawn as well. Power is distributed by a Tremec seven-speed dual clutch automatic. Operated by paddles, your pulls go straight to the transmission controller without a detour through the powertrain control module, massively improving response. It also uses what's called magnetorheological dampers. These units are filled with a liquid, and that liquid is littered with particles of iron. Also housed in the dampers are sets of electromagnets, whose currents influence and manipulate the iron particles to adjust the fluid viscosity, thereby changing the damping and ride character. The GT500 takes all the brutish charm of the original and adds the best of the modern world's fun and fancy tricks.

By 1970, the pony car race was already on, with Ford and Chevrolet battling for supremacy in this new market. Dodge was stuck on the sidelines. It knew it needed to get into the game, and it needed to do it fast. When the first Challenger debuted in 1970, it was clear that Chrysler and Dodge had taken an approach that was a bit of a headscratcher. Rather than making a purpose built pony car, the Challenger was a jack of all trades, attempting to swipe customers from all corners of the performance market.

Regardless of what it wanted to be, the original Challenger was certainly something to behold. It was exciting just to look at, with its muscular haunches and angry face, but all that car did translate to a lot of weight, 3,890 pounds to be exact. Dodge reasoned that it had to be big to make a statement on the road but also to maximize interior space, which it felt was lacking in its competitors' entries. While Dodge got what it wished for in a comfortable and commanding car, the driving dynamics suffered heavily, literally, from the Challenger's heft. Understeer was unavoidable, thanks to its weight, a sore point for the joking boat comparisons Dodge products still endure today. However, the R/T model was fitted with a pushrod V8 that made a whopping 425 horsepower. That alone made it extremely desirable and easy to forgive.

More than 50 years after the release of the original Dodge Challenger, the nameplate had solidified itself as one of America's most rowdy pony cars. Over the years, the Challenger got more powerful and more ridiculous. In 2015, we got the Hellcat, a 707-horsepower supercharged beast that shot the Challenger into legend status, with each subsequent version being somehow more obscene.

Much to our delight, it seems like Dodge wants to bring back the Hellcat V8, but the Demon SRT 170 is currently the final entry in the Hellcat family tree. The elephant, or Demon in the room, is the car's 1,025-horsepower output, making its V8 one of the most powerful 8-cylinder engines ever made. How does a road car get that, you ask? The answer is a 6.2-liter V8 with a supercharger and a hunger for E85 fuel with 170-proof ethanol, hence its name. So powerful is the Demon, that the rear axle and driveshaft had to be upgraded to safely handle its horses and 945 pound-feet of torque. Its eight-speed gearbox is specially designed with a transmission brake for drag racing, allowing rocket-like launches for the quarter mile, with Dodge claiming a 0-to-60 time of just 1.66 seconds. In truth, the Demon 170 goes beyond the original understanding of what a pony car can be. It is a quarter-mile drag racer with a warranty and a price tag guaranteeing the Challenger a place in the history books.

By 1967, Ford was already two years into its newfound stride with the Mustang. Chevrolet was behind, and likely a bit annoyed, because the Mustang had scalped customers from Chevrolet's Corvair market. Chevy had gambled on a car that focused more on lightness, agility, and introducing turbocharging to the masses in the Corvair, and the Mustang served as a rude awakening that American buyers merely wanted something that looked cool and drove fast. Chevy quickly caught up though, and released the new Camaro in 1967.

Compared to the almost European-looking Corvair, the Camaro was an entirely different beast. Chevrolet went all-out for the aggressive look, with the car measuring up at 185 inches long, much of which was taken up by a massive hood. Its grille was flat and wide, and higher trim models like the SS included extra cosmetic enhancements, along with performance upgrades. The SS, standing for Super Sport, featured the biggest V8s in the Camaro lineup, with the crowning version being the L78 396, making 375 horsepower, all of which was sent to the rear wheels. Suspension was upgraded as well, making the SS a truly well-rounded opponent for the Ford's Mustang, and helping the nameplate dig in for what would become a years-long pony car rivalry.

Fast forward to 2024, and the Camaro SS nameplate was still going, but not for much longer. Introduced in 2016, the sixth-generation Camaro would prove to be the last entry in Chevrolet's pony car lineage, at least for now, with the 2024 model year being the last of that last generation. The SS lived on until the very end, though, and in its final form, it was truly something special, bridging the gap between entry-level Camaros and top-trim monsters like the ZL1. Even as a mid-level Camaro, the car still boasted 455 horsepower straight from a no-frills V8.

The V8 in question came with 6.2 liters of displacement, no forced induction, and a pushrod cam setup. To get the most out of the SS, though, you could opt for the 1LE performance package. This added a ton of fun bits and pieces like exclusive black wheels, Recaro racing seats, powerful Brembo brakes, and an adjustable exhaust system that could take the car's roaring V8 siren song from rebellious to rambunctious. Perhaps the coolest thing about the sixth-generation SS, though, was that it could be had not only with a six speed manual transmission, but also with a soft-top body style, giving you wind in the hair and a V8 soundtrack for the ears.

By 1969, the Ford Mustang had fallen into stride as the king of the pony car market and one of Ford's most beloved models. The lineup had grown to envelope entry-level Mustangs all the way up to things like the Boss 429. There was seemingly a Mustang for everyone, and in 1969, Ford decided to enter a new trim called the Mach 1 to serve as a middle-ground ambassador for the Mustang family. The Mach 1 sat in the goldilocks zone of Mustang performance — not too little to be fun, but not too much to be ridiculous, and that was all thanks to its engine.

The Mach 1 had six engine options, with the two most exciting options being the Cobra Jet V8s at the top of the line. This duo of engines both put out 335 horses and were identical in every way except for one using a ram-air function. Despite only one engine option actually needing it, both cars wore a hood scoop that contributed to the car's flashy looks (though only the ram-air model's scoop was functional). Despite its handsome face, the Mach 1 weighed 3,607 pounds, and 59.3% of that weight was on the front wheels. As a rear wheel drive car, this made putting the power down a bit of an issue and detracted from traction and stability. Still, the Mach 1 blended the best of each side of the Mustang spectrum, and it remained undeniably cool.

52 years after the release of the original Mach 1, we saw the final and most recent version of the trim on the S550 generation mustang. A lot has changed in 52 years, but the Mach 1's purpose and place on the Mustang food chain remained the same. When it came out in 2021, the Mach 1 actually replaced three middle ground trim levels in the GT350, the Mustang Bullitt, and the Mustang GT with Performance Package 2. This left a lot of open ground to cover for the Mach 1, with Ford trying to make a modern pony car you could live with, commute in, and even take on the track.

Trying to achieve that perfect blend, the Mach 1 ends up pulling lots of parts from the bins of the three cars it replaced. At the heart of the Mach 1 is a 5.0-liter V8 making 480 horsepower, the same engine that powered the Bullitt. Putting that power to the pavement is a Tremec TR-3160 six-speed manual transmission, sourced from the GT350, with an automatic rev-matching system for perfect downshifts, although it can be disabled for expert drivers. The Mach 1 borrows its front and rear subframes from the GT350 as well, and it uses Ford's fancy adjustable magnetorheological dampers for pinpoint ride control. The underbody also features tons of carved out air channels to help cool anything that gets hot, including the six piston Brembo brakes.

#5815. Fairview Health Services Partners with hellocare.ai to Expand Enterprise Virtual Care and Bring Connected Care to the NICU

Fairview Health Services Partners with hellocare.ai to Expand Enterprise Virtual Care and Bring Connected Care to the NICU" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

Minneapolis, MN and Clearwater, FL — Fairview Health Services and hellocare.ai today announced an enterprise partnership to expand virtual care capabilities across Fairview’s inpatient environments, including a dedicated deployment designed to connect NICU patients, families, and care teams.

As part of the initiative, Fairview is deploying hellocare.ai Module on AI-Assisted Virtual Nursing and Telehealth and AI-Assisted Virtual Sitting through fixed intelligent room devices across inpatient settings. Fairview is also deploying hellocare.ai mobile carts to extend telehealth capabilities wherever virtual clinical support is needed.

Together, these technologies create a flexible enterprise virtual care infrastructure that enables remote clinicians to connect directly with patients and bedside teams, supports virtual nursing workflows, expands patient observation capabilities, and provides on-demand telehealth access throughout the hospital.

“Technology has the greatest impact when it makes care more accessible to our patients while supporting the care teams delivering it,” said Sameer Badlani, MD, Executive Vice President, Chief Digital & AI Officer and Chief New Markets Officer at Fairview. “By creating a scalable virtual care infrastructure across our inpatient environments, we can bring clinical expertise closer to the bedside and continue exploring new ways to use digital technology and AI to improve the care experience.”

Fairview is also deploying hellocare.ai Module on NICU – Family Visits, Baby Observation and Virtual Consults across its NICUs, extending the virtual care experience to some of the health system’s most vulnerable patients and their families.

The NICU solution enables authorized family members to securely connect with and see their baby remotely when they cannot physically be at the bedside, helping families remain connected throughout the NICU journey. The same platform enables virtual consultations, allowing specialists and other members of the care team to remotely connect with the NICU bedside and collaborate on patient care.

“For families with a baby in the NICU, staying connected is incredibly important,” said Darlene Spiegelberg, MAN, BSN, RN, Executive Vice President, Chief Nursing Executive and Acute Operations Officer at Fairview. “This technology gives us another way to bring families closer to their babies while also strengthening collaboration between bedside nurses, specialists, and the broader care team. Expanding our virtual care capabilities also gives our care teams additional tools to deliver safe, high-quality care to patients.”

hellocare.ai’s enterprise platform brings virtual nursing, telehealth, virtual sitting, AI-assisted patient observation, and specialized clinical workflows onto a unified technology platform designed to integrate into existing hospital operations.

“We are proud to partner with Fairview on an enterprise virtual care strategy that extends from the inpatient room to the NICU,” said Labinot Bytyqi, Founder and CEO of hellocare.ai. “Fairview is demonstrating how a unified virtual care platform can support clinicians, improve patient safety, and create meaningful connections between patients, families, and care teams. #5814. Avoiding Chemo in Breast Cancer; Psychedelic Medication for Depression

— Also in TTHealthWatch: treatment of Achilles tendinitis

TTHealthWatch is a weekly podcast from Texas Tech. In it, Elizabeth Tracey, director of electronic media for Johns Hopkins Medicine in Baltimore, and Rick Lange, MD, president of Texas Tech Health El Paso, look at the top medical stories of the week.

This week's topics include treatment of Achilles tendinitis, avoiding chemo in some types of breast cancer, imaging and cardiac stent placement, and a psychedelic medication in depression.

2:38 Treatment-resistant depression and psychedelic medicine

3:38 Three dosages and psychological support

4:38 Adverse events same among all groups

7:00 One in 13 people have Achilles tendinopathy

8:00 Initial improvement with steroids then rapid decline

9:10 HER2-positive early breast cancer giving chemo a miss

11:10 A third responded just to antibodies

Elizabeth: Can we avoid chemotherapy in some women with HER2-positive breast cancer?

Rick: Are injections helpful for people with Achilles tendon problems?

Elizabeth: Can we use a psychedelic medication to help treatment-resistant depression?

Rick: And using imaging to guide stent placement in people with coronary artery disease.

Elizabeth: That's what we're talking about this week on TTHealthWatch, your weekly look at the medical headlines from Texas Tech University Health Sciences Center in El Paso. I'm Elizabeth Tracey, a Baltimore-based medical journalist.

Rick: And I'm Rick Lange, president of Texas Tech Health El Paso.

Elizabeth: Rick, how about if we turn right to the New England Journal of Medicine? This study appears to me to be having some rather large implications for clinical practice.

Rick: This is for people that are going to have a percutaneous coronary intervention because they have coronary artery disease. If you do additional imaging during the procedure, you actually get a better result. That imaging is usually intravascular ultrasound. Use of intravascular imaging is associated with a lower risk of adverse clinical events that require an additional procedure. You don't really have all the data until you're actually in the middle of the procedure.

Well, a lot of people now are getting the coronary CT. It can provide a non-invasive assessment of the coronary artery disease. Since that's done before the procedure, can we use that information to guide therapy? Will it be as useful as using intravascular ultrasound?

So this was an international randomized non-inferiority trial; 1,100 patients that had had coronary CT and they knew they needed to have a procedure done. Half of them were randomized to just using that information to guide stenting. And the other half, in addition, had intravascular ultrasound. And they assessed at 12 months what the rate of target vessel failure was. Those in the CTA [CT angiography] group, about 4.1% had target vessel failure. In the intravascular ultrasound, about 4.6%. The CT was non-inferior to the intravascular ultrasound.

Elizabeth: And a lot easier to do, sounds like, in providing this information a priori versus having it concomitant with the procedure.

Rick: It is, Elizabeth. It requires several things. You have the expertise and the equipment to do this and do it well. Number two is, remember, it exposes the people to radiation. Now, what the study didn't do was it didn't do a cost analysis.

Elizabeth: That, of course, was going to be exactly my next question. And it just seems to me, and I could be wrong on this, but, gosh, CT is just so routine and so quick that I suspect it's less expensive. But I don't know that.

Rick: Yeah. And the other thing I should mention, Elizabeth, this was done at elective procedures.

Elizabeth: OK. Let's turn from here to JAMA, this issue of treatment-resistant depression, a single intranasal administration of the psychedelic mebufotenin for treatment-resistant depression.

This medicine, I should note, is actually a synthetic modification of this toad-derived venom that we've known for a long time has actually had these properties. In this case, they looked at this in participants who were 18 to 75 years of age with moderate to severe major depressive disorder that had been nonresponsive to previous attempts, two to five of them, to treat it with current antidepressant medicines. They were looking at two different dosages of this medicine, as I mentioned, administered intranasally, 8 mg and 12 mg. And their comparator was a 0.3 mg administration alongside with psychological support.

Their primary endpoint was a total score change in the Montgomery-Åsberg Depression Rating Scale from baseline to day 29. And then they had a number of secondary endpoints. They also note that their discharge readiness in comparison with other psychedelic medications, like psilocybin for example, was assessed starting 90 minutes after their dosing.

Basically, what they found, it was a little bit curious. This medicine did seem to have an impact. They called it durable. Their day 29 response rates were 35%, 34%, and 12% with regard to 8 mg, 12 mg, and the comparator 0.3 mg dose. Their remission rates were 26%, 18%, and 8% in that same dosing regimen. It's a little curious, isn't it? Because the 12 [mg] appears to have not quite as good results as the 8 mg dose. They also did note that there were adverse events, but these were more or less the same among all of the doses. The editorialist opines that in comparison to what we already know about things like ketamine and psilocybin, maybe this is something that might add to the armamentarium.

Rick: These individuals, to test the effect of the drug, had to be off their antidepressants. These are people that already have refractory depression. They take them off their antidepressants and they only treat them with this, and then they follow them over the course of 60 days. The fact that a third had some response and a fourth had complete remission, for somebody that has refractory depression and on no other antidepressants, they may actually not be bad results.

Once you treat people with a psychedelic, whether it be this or psilocybin or LSD, you have to observe them until the psychedelic effects wear off. With the other drugs, it's 4 to 12 hours to have to be sitting around waiting. With this particular medication, most people go home in 2 hours. With regard to durability, it lasted for at least 60 days, a single dose. Pretty darn good.

Will it last longer than 60 days? What is the best dose strategy? What if you combine it with other antidepressants? And the last thing I would want to say, Elizabeth, is the people that were excluded from this study were people that have suicidal ideation because there's concern that the psychedelic drugs in individuals with depression and suicidal ideation may actually make those worse.

Elizabeth: The editorialist, of course, also points out the suicidality as an issue, as an exclusion criterion in this trial. So those people clearly need to be examined and studied carefully. The editorialist notes that the average patient became only about a third better. Remission rates were below those typically seen with ketamine and ECT [electroconvulsive therapy]. So since those things exist already, maybe it's important to look really carefully at the practicality of another treatment strategy here.

Rick: Without direct head-to-head comparisons, patients could be different. We would actually need to compare them head to head. The other therapies you mentioned require some expertise and some equipment sometimes. If you could pop someone into your office, give them an intranasal application of a drug that could be effective, even if only in a quarter of individuals, and people would be gone in 2 hours, that's at least another tool in our armamentarium of treating major depression.

Rick: I was unaware that as many as one in 13 individuals have Achilles tendinopathy sometimes. Although exercise treatment is oftentimes recommended, about half the individuals do not get better and almost half these people end up getting additional treatments such as injections. They're putting 50 mL of saline between the Achilles tendon and what's called Kager's fat pad.

These injections sometimes have just saline, sometimes they have steroids, and sometimes they have a local anesthetic. And the thought is that there's a mechanical or ischemic disruption of the pain signaling and the steroid has anti-inflammatory effects. Is it really effective? Nobody has ever tested that before.

So 192 adults with Achilles tendinopathy received a sham small-dose injection, the high-volume injection with steroids, or a high-volume injection without steroids. And then they followed them about a year. There were no clear differences between the sham and the high-volume injections, either with or without steroids. It looked like there was an initial improvement in the people that got injections with steroids, but then there was a rapid decline.

However, when they looked at cost-effectiveness, it looked like the high-dose injection with corticosteroids was cost-effective. I kind of scratched my head and said, gosh, if there's no difference, how could that be more cost-effective? Well, during that initial 12 weeks where it looked like it was a little bit better, that's when people were able to return to work earlier. Even though at the end there was no difference, the fact that they were able to return to work a little bit earlier made it a little bit more cost-effective.

Elizabeth: Sounding like it's back to the drawing board for folks with this condition. I'm wondering, does it talk about the natural history of it? How long does it take to resolve in most people in the absence of treatment?

Rick: Really interesting, because they follow these individuals over the course of about a year. Most of the improvement occurred, even in those that had sham, somewhere between 3 and 6 months. It's a long time. The primary treatment is exercise and anti-inflammatory medications. Those take 3 to 6 months to work, so people have to be patient.

Elizabeth: Let's turn to Nature Medicine and let's look at this idea that, gosh, there are some women who might be able to forego chemotherapy in their HER2-positive early breast cancer. This is a trial that's been ongoing for a while and this is looking at the 5-year outcomes. The study initiated as a noncomparative phase II trial evaluating PET-guided pathological complete response [pCR]-adapted adaptation strategy to omit chemotherapy in women with HER2-positive early breast cancer. I say early, that was stages I through IIIA, and the breast cancer was operable. They were randomized to receive chemotherapy plus trastuzumab [Herceptin] and pertuzumab [Perjeta], or some of them actually ended up getting early chemotherapy, but just a couple rounds of it, and then endocrine therapy.

In the second group, their treatment was adapted according to their FDG-PET response after 2 cycles of chemotherapy and pCR. They previously reported that this de-escalation revealed a 3-year invasive disease-free survival of 94.3%. Here, they're looking at 5-year results using circulating tumor DNA findings.

After their median follow-up of 5.6 years, that number was almost 90%, 89.5% in that group who were randomized to have their circulating tumor DNA assessed along with the FDG-PET results. They only showed in that group one distant recurrence. What they're suggesting is that this might be a really important strategy for being able to look at women who might be able to forego that chemotherapy.

Rick: Standard therapy is you give chemotherapy with [a taxane and a platinum], and you also combine these HER2 antibodies, the two that you mentioned. OK. Maybe we can forego the chemotherapy if, in fact, people would just respond to the HER2 antibodies. That's what they showed. And about a third of those patients did respond just to the antibodies and it saved them the toxic side effects of chemotherapy. This is pretty amazing. Anytime we can minimize the toxicity, get a terrific result, that's great news.

Elizabeth: They do note that this notion of circulating tumor DNA at baseline or during treatment, when they were able to find out, was associated with inferior disease-free survival. What this suggests to me is that looking for the tumor's DNA in the blood has to really be employed as a clinical marker for both "this might be a strategy that's going to work for you" as well as "what's going on on an ongoing basis."

Rick: Yeah. And so, Elizabeth, you're right. They use two different techniques. One is imaging. The other used serum biomarkers. If your imaging looked like the tumor had resolved and there were no biomarkers, those were the best outcomes.

Elizabeth: I'm going to go out on a limb here and prognosticate that at some point, I think, that circulating tumor DNA will supplant imaging because, as we're well aware, frequently imaging misses a lot of metastasis in particular that can be in certain spots in the body where it's difficult to discern.

Rick: And I would suggest that both will be helpful.

Elizabeth: I think both for a while, and I'm guessing it will supplant. We'll see what happens.

On that note then, that's a look at this week's medical headlines from Texas Tech. I'm Elizabeth Tracey.

Rick: And I'm Rick Lange. Y'all listen up and make healthy choices.

#5813. 7 Sleek Sports Cars Ranked Worst To Best By Drag Coefficient

Equipping a sports car with a big and powerful engine is all well and good. But if the car in question is designed like a cinder block, then it's just wasting the engine's potential. As a car speeds up, the air resistance around it increases. And a car with a sleeker design can slip through the air with less resistance, thus granting it better performance. That, in a very basic nutshell, is why aerodynamics matter.

Now, drag coefficient (Cd) isn't the be-all and end-all when it comes to measuring a car's aerodynamics as a whole. Something like drag area, which combines that metric with frontal area measurements, provides a more complete picture. Nevertheless, drag coefficient scores still provide a solid impression as to just how slippery a car is — and such figures are more readily available from automakers, too.

Sleek designs certainly aren't reserved exclusively for performance models; economy cars like Honda's little hybrid that could, the Insight, can also be marvelously slippery. But this article will be focusing on some of the sleekest sports and performance cars out from across the last century, covering old-school favorites such as the Tatra T87 with modern marvels like Volkswagen's XL1.

This Czechoslavkian masterpiece is a genuinely fascinating piece of design. Before moving onto the aerodynamic aspects of the T87, it's first worth covering what else makes it such an intriguing automobile. Motivation is sourced from a rear-engined 2.9-liter V8, which kicked out an impressive-for-the-era 85 horsepower. Back in the '40s, that was a serious amount of power to be dealing with, and Tatra ensured its effectiveness by complimenting it with a seriously slippery design.

German Zeppelins provided plenty of influence behind the T87's iconic shape, and the end result was a drag coefficient of just 0.36 Cd. This enabled the 85-horse V8 to propel the T87 to an impressive 100 mph, although the handling characteristics of a rear-engined machine with independent swing-axle suspension resulted in a fair number of accidents. Rumor has it that, due to so many Nazi officers meeting their maker in T87 accidents, the car was actually banned for use – but the accuracy of these claims has been contested over the years. Still, it all adds to the fascinating history of Tatra's aerodynamic masterpiece.

Production spanned from 1936 to 1950, albeit with a gap during the war years. Despite such a wide production window, though, just over 3,000 T87s were ever built. It proved to be a significant influence to Ferdinand Porsche, and today, it's a cherished classic that attracts collectors willing to pay over $100,000.

The Huayra replaced the awesome Zonda in 2011, and it boasted a design that was just as striking. It was a million-dollar masterpiece at launch, packing a 720-horsepower twin-turbocharged 6.0-liter V12, capable of propelling it along to a top speed of 224 mph. Aerodynamic trickery helps the Italian to remain stable at speed, with front- and rear-mounted flaps that rise and fall to alter downforce levels.

It's important to remember that a supercar like this needs to be comfortable performing through the corners as well as the straight lines. Here's where that active aero really proves its relevancy. Those four flaps allow the Huayra to transform itself depending on the given requirements. While flat, the Huayra boasts a drag coefficient of just 0.31 Cd (as proven by a Mercedes wind tunnel). But they can also flip up to assist the car with braking and keep it planted through the corners.

Much like Pagani did with the Zonda, as the Huayra began to age, the automaker began to produce numerous special editions. Among them was a rolling $7.3 million air piece dubbed the Codalunga. The svelte model sports various ducts and diffusers, plus a longtail design – which is a known method of reducing the amount of drag a car's body produces. However, the Codalunga has not been individually tested in a wind tunnel, so whether it beats the standard Huayra's 0.31 Cd isn't officially known.

While on the topic of longtail designs, it seems appropriate to mention the McLaren Speedtail. This car categorically proves the effectiveness of such a design, with a drag coefficient of just under 0.29 Cd. The British firm from Woking knows a thing or two about churning out slippery supercars, but this Speedtail is something of a caricature; it sits 3 feet longer than the F1, and it's even longer than the F1 GTR Longtail. Helping it cut through the air as precisely as possible is a narrow frontal area, numerous concealed ducts, a complete lack of rear-view mirrors, and front wheels that are almost entirely enclosed.

Of course, a sleek design still needs to be complimented with a mighty power train if impressive performance is the end goal. And with a turbocharged 4.0-liter V8 that combines its efforts with a single electric motor to produce 1,035 horsepower, the Speedtail recipe is certainly a comprehensive one. Combined with a dry weight of just 3,153 pounds, that's enough to see the Speedtail achieve a top speed of 250 mph. Plus, it'll crack 186 mph in just shy of half the time required by its forefather, the mighty F1.

As impressive as the McLaren Speedtail's design is, what's arguably far more impressive is that a $44,245 Corvette from 2005 can match the $2.25 million British hypercar's drag coefficient. With a drag coefficient of just 0.28 Cd, the C6 Chevy is surprisingly slippery. This wasn't a one-hit-wonder for Chevrolet, either, as previous generations had also proven to be remarkably aerodynamic as well. But the C6 manages to outdo them all (albeit only marginally). The C4 boasted a drag coefficient of 0.34 Cd, while the C5 sat at 0.29 Cd. It's worth noting that later generations – including the current C8 — also sit behind the C6's rating.

It's no wonder that people think the C6 is still the best Corvette to date. Regardless of whether you agree or not, it's hard to find real fault with the C6. It combined a brilliantly efficient design with supercar-rivaling performance; the most powerful iteration was the 638-horsepower ZR1, which could top 200 mph. Even the base models were serious performers thanks to an LS1 lurking beneath that low-slung hood. These cars were affordable when new, and they're still great bang-for-buck choices today, with entry-level coupes and convertibles both available for sub-$25,000 – proving that slippery sports cars don't exclusively belong in six-figure price brackets.

Electric cars and hybrids pay a lot of attention to aerodynamics, as being able to slip through the air with minimal resistance is a particularly effective way of increasing a vehicle's range. That's led to buyers of electrified vehicles becoming understandably obsessed with realistic and effective ranges. It should come as no surprise, then, that BMW's bold hybridized i8 sports a drag coefficient of just 0.26 Cd.

That drag coefficient proves that the i8's striking design isn't all about stealing the attention of passers by, in fact, it's really quite clever. The various slices and slashes between those layered body panels help to direct airflow into the car's various radiators, which allows the i8 to disregard active aero. Even the cockpit itself is teardrop-shaped to reduce drag, while the flared rear pillars help keep the visuals sweet without damaging any aerodynamic benefits.

With a turbocharged 1.5-liter inline-three engine and single electric motor tackling the task of motivation, the i8's power train recipe could not be more different from that of the aforementioned Corvette. However, just like the C6, the BMW i8 now finds itself at a very tempting price point, with early examples now changing hands for sub-$40,000.

This one's probably something of a surprise, as unlike so many of the other mentions on this list, the Nissan GT-R doesn't exactly look immensely slippery. It's not particularly low-slung, it doesn't incorporate an obvious longtail design, nothing else about it is clearly geared toward aerodynamics — plus, there's a great big spoiler adorning the trunk. However, that hasn't stopped the GT-R from being a technological marvel with a drag coefficient of only 0.26 Cd. Yep, this chunky model with heaps of boost and gaping grills matches the rating of BMW's slippery little eco-minded coupe.

The secrets of the GT-R low drag coefficient are actually somewhat hidden. It sports an almost completely flat floor, a functional diffuser which helps to channel airflow efficiency, and a slightly tapered rear overhang. Also helping to direct the air in an effective manner are what Nissan describes as "aero-blades" adorning the front fenders, while the narrow fender vents help to provide valuable downforce at the front, too.

Throughout its impressive 18-year tenure, the R35 GT-R saw the power from its twin-turbocharged 3.8-liter V6 rise to genuine supercar levels. And the clever aero tweaks it received over those years helped drivers to make the most of that strength. It came incredibly close to cracking the 7-minute barrier on the Nurburgring, peaking with a time of 7:08.679 in its 2013 Nismo guise — breaking the world record for fastest volume production car in the process.

All of the cars featured upon this list are aerodynamically impressive, and they certainly sit a long way removed from the least aerodynamic cars ever made. However, the Volkswagen XL1 stands in a class of its own. The sole purpose of this striking little hybridized-diesel inline-three-powered sports car was to be as mightily efficient as possible.

The headline number here is a drag coefficient of just 0.19 Cd. To get this number down so far, it combines many of the other engineering techniques used by other cars on this list. It very obviously sports a teardrop profile like the i8, allowing the smoothest possible path for airflow. Like the GT-R, the car's floor is completely flat, preventing the underside from pushing against the wind. And — going above and beyond the Speedtail in this regard – covered rear wheels assist the XL1 in achieving its remarkably low drag coefficient.

It wasn't just aerodynamic efficiency that Volkswagen was chasing with the XL1. It was also designed to be immensely frugal on fuel, to the point where a Honda Insight or Toyota Prius might look like a big-block Chevy from the '70s in comparison. On the European combined test cycle, Volkswagen managed to achieve a frankly mind-boggling 313 mpg, a feat helped by the model's incredibly low curb weight (courtesy of magnesium wheels and a carbon-fiber monocoque chassis).
